spans.t: This is a small book to be read slowly. It has thirty readings and each takes about five minutes. Read one a day, or one at the end of each stage, or open it anywhere and read what falls open. Nobody is counting.
Every reading has the same four parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from
The Imitation of Christ
, a book of the inner life written in Latin about six hundred years ago. The words are quoted exactly as the translator, William Benham, gave them in 1886,
thee
and
thou
and all. Read the passage twice. The second time, read it aloud if you can, even under your breath. Old English slows the eye down, and that is half of its use.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Thomas's. It starts from something on the road, a bench, a bell, a blister, and lets the passage open it. It tries to say plainly what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. You will not need a notebook. Most of them are better done on your feet.
A short prayer.
Original and short. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish, to nobody in particular, and see how it sounds in your own mouth.

spans.t: A Christian book, and who it is for
The Imitation of Christ

is a Christian book. It speaks to its reader as a believer, and in several places it speaks as Christ himself. We say so plainly so that nobody is surprised. People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All of them are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Thomas believed to recognise what he noticed about tiredness, pride, silence and the wish to begin again. Where he is hard to follow, we say so and do not pretend otherwise.
The shape of the book
The readings do not follow the order of the original. They follow a walk, from setting out to coming home, in ten movements:

items.t: Readings 1 to 4,
setting out
: a good beginning, a stranger's lightness, the limits of any guide, and not going faster than you can.
Readings 5 to 7,
the weight we carry
: what we carry, what we could put down, and what makes a load lighter.
Readings 8 to 10,
silence
: listening, the wandering mind, and a prayer with no words.
Readings 11 to 13,
weariness
: small things that wear us down and what to do on a flat day.
Readings 14 to 16,
companions
: the people we share a room and a road with.
Readings 17 to 20,
doubt
: fear of the end, changing moods, tomorrow's worries and the long wait.
Readings 21 and 22,
how we measure
: what we count, and what other people say.
Readings 23 and 24,
gratitude
: small gifts and the road as a book.
Readings 25 to 27,
arrival
: the shrine, the day after, and being at home.
Readings 28 to 30,
return
: carrying the Way into an ordinary week.

spans.t: A movement is only a few days' worth, but the book does not need thirty days. Skip, repeat, read backwards. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
On the road and at home

Read on a bench, in a bunk, in a café while the soup arrives. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. The practices are deliberately small: a breath, a step count, a greeting. They are meant to be done without turning the walk into a task.

At home the book works the same way. Read one in the evening and carry the question through the next day, on the bus or at a desk. Pilgrims often say that the harder walk begins when they get back. The last movement of the book is for that.
A few words you will meet:
albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks, often with a communal kitchen.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly "have a good Way". Both are used here without fuss.
Read slowly. The classic is old, and it was written to be read slowly, one line at a time, by people with a long day ahead of them.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man
The Imitation of Christ
is traditionally, and now generally, attributed to Thomas à Kempis. He was born about 1380 in Kempen, a small town near the Rhine in what is now Germany, which is where the
à Kempis

comes from: "of Kempen". He grew up in the Low Countries, in a reforming movement of the time called the Modern Devotion, which cared less for learned argument than for a plain, steady inner life. He joined a community of canons regular at Mount Saint Agnes, near Zwolle, in what is now the Netherlands. Canons regular are priests who live together under a rule. He spent most of his long life there, copying manuscripts, reading and writing, and he died in 1471.

We know little else with certainty, and we will not pretend to. Scholars have debated the authorship of the book for centuries. The introductory note in the English edition we use mentions, among other names once put forward, Bernard of Clairvaux, the English writer Walter Hilton and the Parisian chancellor Jean Gerson, and calls Thomas the most probable author. That is still the common view. A reader who prefers to say "the author" is not wrong.
The book

The Imitation was written in Latin, in the 1420s. It was copied by hand in great numbers, translated into many languages, and printed from the later fifteenth century on. The edition we use opens with a note that says that, apart from the Bible, no Christian writing has had so wide a following. The title comes from the heading of its first chapter, "Of the imitation of Christ".
It comes in four short books, each with its own heading in this edition:

items.t: The first book,
Admonitions profitable for the spiritual life
: plain counsel on humility, silence, patience and bearing with other people.
The second book,
Admonitions concerning the inner life
: how to live from within, and what to do when comfort goes away.
The third book,
On inward consolation

: the most loved of the four. It is written as a conversation. A voice, which the book means as Christ's, speaks to the reader as "My Son", and the disciple answers. When a reading is taken from such a passage, the reflection says who is speaking.
The fourth book,
Of the Sacrament of the Altar
: on Holy Communion. Two readings use lines from it that speak of patience and of shrines. We have not tried to explain or discuss the Sacrament. It belongs to those who share the author's faith.

spans.t: Why it suits a pilgrim

The book calls its reader a stranger and a pilgrim in more than one place. It is not about a destination. It is about how to walk: how to begin, what to do when you are tired, how to be among people, how to bear a bad day and a good one without being thrown by either. It is made of short chapters and can be read a little at a time. That is why it travelled so well in its own century, and why it can still sit in a pocket.

It is also a hard book, and it is a fifteenth-century book. In places Thomas is more severe with himself than most of us would care to be, and his pages on judgement and punishment, on despising the world and on obedience in a cloister are not here. They are all still in the original for anyone who wants them. We chose the passages that speak most plainly to someone on a road. Thomas writes "man" and "he" for everyone. We have left his words alone, and these readings are for anyone.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The English in the passages is by the Reverend William Benham, published in 1886. Benham and Thomas are both long out of copyright, so the translation is in the public domain. It is available from Project Gutenberg as ebook number 1653, and every quotation in this book was checked against that text, word for word.

What we changed in the passages is nothing. We kept the old spellings and endings, and even a spot or two where the text looks like a printer's slip. We left out the small footnote numbers. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. The choice of the thirty passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours and they are original. Of the thirty, eighteen come from the third book, five from the second, five from the first and two from the fourth.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.

chapters.title: Day 1. A stranger and a pilgrim

spans.t: What do you carry when you are only passing through?
The passage

paras.t: If thou wilt stand fast and wilt profit as thou oughtest, hold thyself as an exile and a pilgrim upon the earth. … Keep thyself as a stranger and a pilgrim upon the earth, to whom the things of the world appertain not. Keep thine heart free, and lifted up towards God, for here have we no continuing city.

spans.t: Reflection

There is a moment, somewhere between your own front door and the first yellow arrow, when you stop being someone who lives somewhere and become someone who is going. The pack is on your back. A shell, if you have one, swings from a strap. In a pocket is the
credencial
, the folded pilgrim passport that will collect a stamp in every town. Nothing has happened yet. You are simply no longer where you were.

Thomas à Kempis had words for that state, and he did not keep them for people with rucksacks. He thought they described every reader. A stranger and a pilgrim, an exile and a pilgrim: someone away from home who has not yet arrived anywhere that stays.

The lines look severe at first. Keep yourself like a visitor, he says, to whom the things of the world do not belong. Keep the heart free and lifted up. For here, in his old phrase, we have no continuing city. No place lasts. Every town you walk through will carry on without you tomorrow, and so will the one you left behind.

Read on a road, it is gentler than it sounds. A walker already lives this way. You own what fits in the pack, and you chose it with care because you must carry it. You sleep in beds that are not yours and wake in rooms you will not see again. You are a guest in every village, and the best guests tidy up after themselves and say thank you. There is a lightness in it that anyone who has walked for a few days will know: the surprise of how little is needed, and how much of what weighed on you at home was never in the bag.

Leaving is its own small labour. On the first morning nearly everyone pats their pockets three times: passport, phone, money, water. The checking is natural, and it is also a tiny rehearsal of the clenched fist, the wish to make the day safe by holding on to everything that might go wrong. Somewhere around the second village the pockets stop being checked. Nothing fell out. The day went on being what it was.

Now the hard part. Thomas wrote for people in a cloister, and "the things of the world do not belong to you" can be heard as coldness, as if the world and the people in it were to be held at arm's length. Most of us have a family, a job, a body that aches. We cannot treat them as scenery, and we should not try. The reading that serves a walker is narrower and kinder. It does not say love nothing. It says hold nothing in a clenched fist. You can love a house, a person, a plan, and still know that the hand holding it should be open. A heart that is free is free to move on because it was never nailed to the last place.

There is an honest doubt to set beside this. It is easy to feel like a stranger on the first morning, when home is a day behind you and one phone call away. The real test of "no continuing city" does not come on the first day. It comes on the afternoon when a place feels so good you would stay for ever, and on the evening when a place feels so bad you would give anything to leave. In both, the same sentence holds: this is not where you live. The good place will end, and so will the bad one. That is a comfort and a small grief together, and it is allowed to be both.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Something modest. To arrive in each place as a guest does, noticing and thanking and claiming nothing. To leave the room a little tidier than you found it. To pass through the afternoon's irritation without moving in. And to remember that "pilgrim" is not a title you earn by distance. In Thomas's hands it is a way of holding yourself, and you can take it up this morning, before you have walked a single kilometre.
For the walk

items.t: What am I holding too tightly this morning: a plan, a worry, a picture of how this walk should feel? Name it, then picture the hand that holds it opening a little.

For the first ten minutes, look at each place you pass as a guest would. Say a silent thank you to the first house, field or person you notice, and claim nothing from any of them. If it helps, choose one word for what you have left behind and let it stay behind.

spans.t: At the end of the day

You have arrived somewhere, or you are about to. The bed is unfamiliar, the pillow is the wrong shape, and somewhere along the room a stranger is zipping and unzipping a bag. Your feet are warm and complaining. For a minute, do nothing at all. The first evening of a long walk is always odd. Your body is tired in places it did not know it had, and your mind is still half at home.

Look back over the day without hurry. Some of it was hard. Perhaps there was a moment in the morning when the whole idea seemed faintly ridiculous. Perhaps there was a long middle stretch where the pack argued with your shoulders, or an hour spent working out what you had forgotten to bring. It may have been lonely, or too crowded. Say what was hard, in one sentence, to yourself. It does not need a solution tonight.

Some of it was good, even if you are too tired to feel it yet. A greeting from someone on the road. The first time you looked up and found you had walked a kilometre without thinking. Water that tasted of something. The smell of a bakery. Say that too.

Today you were a stranger and a pilgrim, both at once. In a new town nobody knows you, and nobody expects you to be anyone in particular. That can be frightening and it can be a relief. Tonight it may be both.

If today was easy, be careful of the opposite mistake. A day does not have to turn into a lesson before it can be allowed to be good. And if there are messages waiting from home, answer them in a sentence if you want to. You are allowed to be a stranger for a little while.
Three small questions for the dark:

items.t: Where did I feel like a guest today, and where did I feel like an owner of something: a place in a queue, a bunk, a view, an opinion?
What did I carry today that I did not need?
What was given to me today that I did not earn?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. You may not be able to answer any of this. The first day costs more than the distance suggests, because the body spends effort on newness alone. If the questions slide off, let them. They will keep until morning, and so will you. Putting the phone down and closing your eyes counts as the last practice of the day.
Down the room the lights go out, one by one. For a few breaths everybody in it is, just for tonight, exactly what Thomas said: a stranger, a pilgrim, a guest of the dark.
A short prayer

Tonight I am a guest in this bed, in this town, in this day. Thank you for the roof and for whoever lit the lamp. Let me hold lightly what I cannot keep, and receive without grabbing what is given. Forgive the day its clumsiness, and mine. Let my body rest and my heart stay open, ready to go on in the morning.

chapters.title: Day 2. The load that carries you

spans.t: Is it the weight that hurts, or the quarrel with it?
The passage

paras.t: If thou willingly bear the Cross, it will bear thee, and will bring thee to the end which thou seekest, even where there shall be the end of suffering; though it shall not be here. If thou bear it unwillingly, thou makest a burden for thyself and greatly increaseth thy load, and yet thou must bear it. If thou cast away one cross, without doubt thou shalt find another and perchance a heavier.

spans.t: Reflection

On the second morning the pack is no heavier than it was on the first. Nobody has added a stone. But yesterday's straps have left their marks, and you now know exactly where the weight sits. This is the day when walkers start to have opinions about it. They heft the pack and judge it. They look at the third paperback, the spare pair of trousers, the little tin that seemed essential in the shop, and they begin to bargain.

Thomas à Kempis was not talking about rucksacks. His word is the Cross, and for him it meant the trouble that comes to anyone who tries to live honestly: illness, loss, disappointment, the people who are hard to love, the days that go against you. His claim is plain. You will carry something. That part is not up to you. What is up to you is how.

Read the middle sentence slowly. If you bear it unwillingly, you make a burden for yourself and greatly increase your load. Most of us know this from the inside. There is the weight itself, and then there is the argument with the weight: why me, why today, why is it not fair. The argument has no mass you could put on a scale, and it still wears you out faster than the thing it is arguing about. Anyone who has walked uphill muttering knows that the muttering does not shorten the hill.

The first sentence has a lovely promise in it: carried willingly, the load will carry you. Walkers say much the same about a well-fitted pack. Done up properly, with the weight low on the hips, the strongest part of you takes it, and the shoulders are left free. The load becomes part of how you move. And a load can bring you to where you are going. The pack holds the bed, the rain jacket and the water. Without it there is no walk at all. The same is true of a day. A day carried willingly, even a hard one, takes you somewhere. A day carried grudgingly only takes you to the evening.

Now say where it is hard, because it is. "Willingly" is the word that snags. Some weights are unjust. Some are too heavy for one person. A person with real grief, or real pain, is not helped by being told to carry it cheerfully, and Thomas is not asking for cheerfulness. Elsewhere in his book he says things about suffering that this reading does not follow. Taken narrowly, the sentence is practical and not pious: what cannot be changed is made heavier by fighting it.

The last sentence deserves a careful look too. If you throw away one cross, you will find another, perhaps heavier. That is not always true. Some loads should be put down, and the wisdom is in telling which. A walker who sends a parcel home at the next post office has done something sensible. But there is a truth in it as well. Many people set out on a long walk hoping to leave something behind, and find it has travelled in the pack. A load thrown away in anger is often picked up again in another shape.

So what does it ask of an ordinary day? Perhaps three small things. First, a morning inventory: which of these weights are really mine, and which am I carrying out of habit, or because I never asked for help? Put down what can be put down. Second, for the weight that cannot be set down today, stop arguing with it, or at least argue more quietly. Say, "This is today's weight." Third, ask someone to take a share. Pilgrims do it all the time with bags, with blisters and with worries. It is a very ordinary habit of the road.

There is an honest doubt left over, and it is better not to hide it. Can anyone decide to be willing? Probably not, on command. But you can begin with the smallest honest step: admit that you are unwilling, loosen a strap, take a breath, and walk on. Willingness may come later, or it may not. A burden carried without a quarrel is already half as heavy.
For the walk

items.t: What am I carrying today that I could put down, and what must I carry whether I like it or not? Name each in a few plain words.

Stop once in the first hour and adjust a single strap, or let your shoulders drop and roll back. As you do it, say quietly, "This is today's weight," and walk on without arguing with it. Notice, later, the first moment when you forget to argue.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The pack is off at last. That first moment of setting it down is one of the small private pleasures of the road: your shoulders float, your back straightens, and for a few minutes you feel strangely light, almost as if you might lift off the floor. Sit with that. It is the nearest thing to a picture of what Thomas is describing.

Look back over the day. What was heavy? There was the pack, certainly, and perhaps a stiff knee, or a hill that went on after it should have stopped. But heaviness comes in other forms, too. A phone call. A remark that is still turning over in your mind. A memory that walked beside you for an hour and would not go away. Name the heaviest thing. Was it the weight itself, or the argument you were having with it?

And what was light? Even a hard day has a few such moments: a downhill stretch, a bench in the shade, someone who offered to carry something, or simply a moment when the load and the walking were one thing and you forgot you were carrying anything at all.

Unpacking is a small ritual of its own. Lay out what you used today and what you never touched. Many walkers find that something has travelled all day without once being needed, and that what they reached for most was small: a warm layer, a pair of dry socks, a number written on paper. The pack tells you honestly what you actually carry.

Heavy days teach the body something too: how much it can bear, and how quickly it recovers once it is allowed to stop. What you could not manage this afternoon may be quite manageable after a night's sleep.
Tonight, three gentle questions:

items.t: What did I argue with today that I might have simply carried?
Is there something in my pack, or in my head, that I could post home or leave behind tomorrow?
Who offered me help today, and who could I ask tomorrow?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Weariness makes everything heavier, including thoughts. The worry that looked enormous at four o'clock often looks smaller after food and a wash, and smaller still after sleep. Do not try to settle the big questions of your life in a bunk bed. Put the pack where you can reach it in the morning, and let it be a pack again, and nothing more.
If any weight is too much to carry alone, say it to somebody tomorrow, in a plain sentence. That is not failure. It is how most loads on this road are carried.
A short prayer

Let me put down what was never mine to carry. Let me carry the rest without a quarrel. Where the load is too much, send a hand, and let me be glad to take it. Tonight the pack is by the bed and my shoulders are light. Let me not carry tomorrow's weight tonight. Let that be enough until morning, and let sleep come easily.
What can you hear when the road goes quiet?
The passage

paras.t: Blessed is the soul which heareth the Lord speaking within it, and receiveth the word of consolation from His mouth. Blessed are the ears which receive the echoes of the soft whisper of God, and turn not aside to the whisperings of this world. Blessed truly are the ears which listen not to the voice that soundeth without, but to that which teacheth truth inwardly.

spans.t: Reflection

Some time in the first hour, if you let it, the road goes quiet. The village is behind you. The last dog has given up. What is left is small: the scuff of your boots, the creak of the pack, a cockerel somewhere that has not been told it is no longer dawn, and perhaps, far off, the hum of a main road that you can never quite place. Then, after a few minutes, you notice there is another kind of noise. It is inside. The conversation you should have had last week. The list for the weekend. The tune that has been playing since breakfast.

Thomas à Kempis opens his third book with this problem. Up to here his chapters give advice. In the third book he changes the form: it becomes a conversation, a voice speaking to the reader, and the reader answering. These words are the beginning of it, and they are the reader speaking, hoping to be spoken to. Blessed are the ears, he says, that take in the echoes of a soft whisper and do not turn aside to the whisperings of this world.

Two kinds of listening are being set side by side. One is the voice that sounds outside: news, opinion, gossip, advertising, the commentary of other people. The other is the voice that teaches from within, and Thomas says it is soft. It does not shout. It has to be listened for, and it cannot be heard over the other.

Everyone who has walked a few hours alone understands the practical sense in that. A morning spent with earphones in is a morning with the world's voice playing on top of your own. There is nothing wicked in it. But the whisper, whatever you take it to be, a conscience, a memory, a calm you had forgotten or God, is not going to compete.

Here is where the passage is harder than it looks. For some people quiet is not gentle. It is the place where the old arguments are kept. If the voice inside you is mostly a critic, then "listen inwards" is not an invitation, and nobody should force it. Thomas has something quieter in mind, the voice that consoles. But it may take days of walking before the critic runs out of breath, and until it does, the quiet can feel crowded. That is not a failure of the practice. It is how the practice begins.

Notice also what he does not say. He does not say that company is bad, or that talk is a sin. A road full of voices, a table shared with strangers, a laugh from the next bunk: these are among the best things on the Way. Thomas is warning against being carried off by whatever speaks loudest. The line he draws is between what pulls at you and what steadies you, and you can hear both from the same bench.

The quiet is not empty, either. A path through fields has more in it than a street does: water in a ditch, wind in a hedge, the tick of a gate, your own steps. You only hear them once you stop talking over them.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? An hour with no input. Not as a discipline or a boast, only as an experiment. Walk without earphones. Let a thought arrive and watch it go by, like a car on a distant road, without climbing in. Listen for the quietest sound you can find, a leaf, a water pipe, your own breath, and stay with it a minute.

And a word of doubt, because this book would rather be honest than soothing. Some mornings nothing comes. The quiet is merely quiet, and the mind is merely busy, and the whisper, if there is one, has nothing to say. Thomas knows this day well. His whole book is full of such days, and it keeps going. Perhaps "blessed" does not mean those who hear clearly. Perhaps it means those who keep their ears turned the right way, and stay on the road, and wait.
For the walk

items.t: What is the quietest thing I can hear right now, and what is the loudest thing in my head? Notice them both. You do not have to change either.

For the first twenty minutes of walking, take no music, no podcast and no conversation. When a thought pulls at you, name it in one word, "plan" or "worry" or "tune", and let it go by. Go back to your steps. If twenty minutes is too many, take ten. The aim is to leave a gap, not to win it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Even in an albergue the evening has its own sounds: water running, a spoon on a plate, three languages in the kitchen, someone laughing at the far end of the table. Then, later, the sounds of sleep, and a few of the less welcome sounds of sleep. This is a good moment to ask what you heard today, outside and in.

Outside, perhaps, there was a lot. Voices on the road, a bell, traffic, birds, the cheerful bustle of a village. Some of it you chose and some of it simply arrived. Some of it, if you are honest, you used to avoid hearing yourself think. That is no sin. Most of us carry a little noise with us in the way we carry a snack.

Inside, what was loudest? Today it might have been planning: tomorrow's distance, tonight's bed, the next meal. It might have been an old conversation, rerun with a better ending. It might have been the voice that says you are slower than everyone, or that you should have stayed at home. Notice it without arguing. A voice that has been named has less power than a voice that has only been obeyed.

And was there ever a quieter one? Often there is, and it is easy to miss: a moment when your breathing matched your steps, when something in the landscape stopped you, when a sentence you had been looking for turned up without being called. If you noticed such a moment today, you were already doing what the passage describes. If you did not, you are not behind.

It is also worth noticing the voices you went looking for. A phone in the pocket is a very small door onto the whole world, and in the evening it is hard not to open it. There is no rule against that. But you might ask whether the last voice you hear tonight should be the world's, or only the room's.
Three questions for the end of a day:

items.t: What was the quietest moment of today, and where was I?
Which voice was loudest in my head, and did I believe it?
Is there anything gentle I noticed today and then walked past?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Evening is a poor time for listening. The body wants food and a flat surface, and the mind plays back the day too fast to follow. Do not force a silence you are too tired to hold. Sometimes the kindest kind of listening is to lie down and let the room be as noisy as it is. If something quiet has to say itself to you, it can wait until the morning, when the road is empty again. If you can manage it, put the phone face down tonight and listen to the room for one minute: the breathing, the pipes, a door, the town beyond the window. That is a very small version of the morning's practice, and it is enough.
A short prayer

In this noisy room, let me find one quiet place. Let what is gentle be heard over what is loud. If there is a word for me tonight, let it be small enough to hear. If there is none, let the silence be enough, and let me sleep inside it. Let the noise of the day settle like dust in a sunbeam, and be still.
What would it mean to begin today as if for the first time?
The passage

paras.t: We ought daily to renew our vows, and to kindle our hearts to zeal, as if each day were the first day of our conversion, and to say, “Help me, O God, in my good resolutions, and in Thy holy service, and grant that this day I may make a good beginning, for hitherto I have done nothing!” … If thou canst not be always examining thyself, thou canst at certain seasons, and at least twice in the day, at evening and at morning. In the morning make thy resolves, and in the evening inquire into thy life, how thou hast sped to-day in word, deed, and thought; for in these ways thou hast often perchance offended God and thy neighbour.

spans.t: Reflection
The best hour of a walking day is very often the first. The
albergue

is dark and full of small sounds: a zip, a rustle of plastic bags, someone trying hard not to wake anyone. You find your boots by feel. Outside, the street is cool and empty, and for a few minutes you have not yet done anything late, slow or wrong. The day is a blank sheet and your hand has not touched it.

By the fourth morning that feeling needs some help. The novelty has worn off. The body has opinions. Yesterday's mood is still lying across the bed like a coat. This is exactly where Thomas à Kempis starts: renew your resolutions every day, he says, as if it were the first day of your new life. And then he gives the reader the words to say.
Help me, O God, in my good resolutions, and grant that this day I may make a good beginning, for hitherto I have done nothing!

That last phrase can sound like despair. Four days walked and a long way still to go, and he says, nothing done? But it helps to read it as a kindness. Yesterday's kilometres do not walk today's. The morning owes you nothing and holds nothing against you. You may start without your score. And notice what he asks for: a good beginning, not a good day. Beginning is the part we can actually do. The day will have its own weather and its own blisters, and it will go as it goes. We can choose the first step, and then the next.

Notice too that the little prayer asks for help. A beginning here is not a clenched effort of will. It starts with admitting that you need some. A reader who does not pray can still use the plain word.
Help me begin.
It costs nothing and it is more honest than most of what we say to ourselves at six in the morning.

The second half of the passage puts a second hinge on the day. Twice at least, he says, at evening and at morning. In the morning make your resolves, and in the evening look back over how the day went in word, deed and thought. That is a very simple structure and it works for walkers: a short beginning, a long walk, and a short look back, like two bookends on a shelf.

Now say where it is hard. The evening part can go sour. A review of "word, deed and thought" can turn into a trial, with the mind as both prosecutor and accused, and a bunk bed for a courtroom. That would defeat the whole purpose, because the morning was meant to lay the score down. The old advice only works if the evening look is as gentle as the morning start. Look at the day as a friend would. Name what went wrong. Then let it sleep with you, not stand over you. If you cannot do it kindly, it is better to leave the review out than to stage it badly.

There is a second difficulty, and it is the common one. Some mornings you will not feel any beginning at all. You will be stiff and a little afraid and wondering why you came. Then a "good beginning" may be nothing more than the act of tying your laces and standing up. That counts. Thomas is asking for a will, not a mood. A mood cannot be summoned, and a will can be small enough to carry out on four hours' bad sleep.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? To start it on purpose. Before the first step, take thirty seconds. Say, in whatever words you like, that you are beginning, and ask for whatever help you think you might need. Then go. It is a small ritual and it changes the feel of the next hour, in the same way that opening a window changes a room.

The passage also works at home. Anyone who has stood in a kitchen at seven on a grey Monday knows how much of life depends on a good beginning, and how much of it is a decision to start again, quietly, without commentary. The road simply makes it easier to see.
For the walk

items.t: If today were the first day of this walk, what would I do differently in the first hour?

Before you take the first step, stand still for three breaths. Say, "Today I begin," in your own words, and ask for whatever help you need, aloud or silently. Then go. Choose one thing you want to begin well today, the first kilometre or the first greeting, and give it your whole attention. If you stumble in the next hour, simply say it again and take the next step.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Somewhere in the last hours you have been in the middle of the day with no clear memory of the morning. That is the shape of most walking days. The beginning is bright and the middle is long, and by the evening the beginning is almost forgotten. So this is a good time to go back to it.

Do you remember how you started? Perhaps you stood a moment and said a few words, or perhaps you only laced your boots and went. Either is a beginning. Now look at the day as a whole, gently, as a friend might who has walked beside you and does not need to be impressed. What went well? Be specific, however small: a good pace for an hour, a kind word to someone, a rest taken when you needed it.

If it helps, give the day a single sentence, the kind you might put on a postcard: "Today I...". Do not polish it. If the sentence is flat, let it be flat. A day does not have to be remarkable to have been walked well.

What went badly? Say that too. Perhaps there was a sharp word, or a stretch where you gave up on the day inside your head, or an afternoon wasted in comparing yourself to someone who walked faster. You do not need to judge it. Name it, and notice that it is already over.

The hardest and most useful thing about beginning again is that it can happen at any hour. If the afternoon went wrong, you did not have to wait until the morning to start over. You could have begun again at the next bench. Notice whether, today, you did.

It is possible, too, to begin the night well. Wash, drink some water, stretch for a minute, and lay out what you will need in the morning. These are very small acts, and they say that the day is being closed with care and not simply dropped.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I begin well today, however small?
Where did I need to begin again, and did I?
What would I like to put down before I sleep, so that I can pick up nothing of it tomorrow?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. You are not in a fit state to make resolutions tonight, and you are not obliged to. Tomorrow's beginning will be there at six, and it will ask for no more than laces and a few words. Tonight the work is the opposite: to let the day end, and be finished. Whatever it was, it has been walked. That is enough.
A short prayer

Thank you for the day that is finished. Forgive its small failures, and mine, and let them stay here when I leave. Let me wake without carrying a score. Give me help for a good beginning tomorrow, and a heart willing to take it. Whatever was left undone tonight, let it be undone, and let me close my eyes without finishing it. Now let me rest.

chapters.title: Day 5. Not more than you are able

spans.t: Is enthusiasm a good guide to how far you can go?
The passage

paras.t: Some who were presumptuous because of the grace of devotion within them, have destroyed themselves, because they would do more than they were able, not considering the measure of their own littleness, but rather following the impulse of the heart than the judgment of the reason. … They who are as yet new and unskilled in the way of the Lord, unless they rule themselves after the counsel of the wise, may easily be deceived and led away.

spans.t: Reflection

The fifth day is one of the dangerous ones, and it does not feel dangerous at all. The first morning was nerves and the second was sore, but by now something has loosened. Your legs have found a rhythm. The pack is a fact. The villages come and go like pages. You feel strong, perhaps stronger than you have felt in years, and the thought arrives, quite reasonably, that you could do a few more kilometres today. Why stop at the planned place? Why not the next one? Other walkers are going on. The light is good.

Walkers who have done this before tend to say the same thing about the early days: they are when the trouble starts. A tendon complains, a shin tightens, a blister gets going under a sock that has been wet for an hour. The advice that is passed from one walker to another is dull and almost always the same. Start shorter than you think you need to. Build slowly. Stop while there is still something left.

Thomas à Kempis says it in his own way, and it is blunter than most. He is writing about people who had a surge of inward fervour, a warmth in their faith, and who rode it too hard. They wanted to do more than they were able, he says, "not considering the measure of their own littleness", and followed the impulse of the heart instead of the judgement of reason. They destroyed themselves, he says. It is a strong word, and he means it as a warning, not a prediction. The same mistake can be made with a knee.

There is nothing wrong with the impulse. It is fuel. The trouble is only that it is a poor map. The heart tells you how much you want to do, and it has no way of telling you how much the body can bear this week. For that you need reason, and reason is the plain, unglamorous business of looking at the actual distance, the actual heat, the actual state of your feet.

The second sentence goes a step further. Those who are new and unskilled in the way, he says, should take the counsel of the wise, or they are easily led astray. On a long walk the wise are not hard to find. They are the people who have walked before, who sit on the same bench at four in the afternoon, rub their ankles and tell you, without lecturing, what they wish they had done. A pharmacist, a host in an
albergue

, a fellow traveller whose pace you trust. What the wise say is rarely deep. Drink more water than you think you need. Eat before you are hungry. Stop a little earlier than you wish. None of it is clever, and all of it works. To take advice from such a person is not weakness. It is a good use of the time they have already spent.

Where is this hard? First, in the phrase "the measure of their own littleness". It can sound like a put-down, and Thomas is not above putting people down. Read it as a measure and not a judgement. Every body has a pace, and so does every mind and every heart. Knowing yours is not smallness. It is the beginning of going far. Second, limits are hard to see from inside. How do you know that what stops you is the body, and not fear dressed up as prudence? There is no rule. But the body's signals are usually clear: a sharp pain, a pain that grows, a tightness that does not warm up. Fear tends to be vaguer and louder. If it is sharp, or if it gets worse, see a pharmacist or a doctor, and in a real emergency call 112. That is not heroism, and it is not defeat.

The word that fits this day is patience, and here it simply means pace. It means believing that a month of ordinary days will take you further than a week of heroic ones. Any day you finish with something in reserve is a day that has made tomorrow possible.
For the walk

items.t: If I were walking for a month and not for a day, would I walk like this?

For the first hour, go a little slower than feels natural. Find a pace at which you could talk, or hum a tune, without gasping. Then notice, when the hour is up, how much easier the second hour feels. At each stop, give your feet ten seconds of honest attention: any new heat, any tightness that has not gone?

spans.t: At the end of the day

Take the boots off first, and then the socks, and sit for a moment with your bare feet on a cool floor. The next few minutes are a conversation with your body, and for once you are the one who should be listening.

Start at the feet and work upwards. Toes, heels, ankles, shins, knees, thighs, hips, back, shoulders. Not as a medical examination, only as an honest question at each stop: how are you? Some places will answer with a dull ache that means they have done their work. A few may say something sharper. If anything is sharp, or hot, or swollen, or worse than it was this morning, make a note to see a pharmacist or a doctor tomorrow before you go on. That is the wise counsel the passage speaks of, and it is available in most towns of any size.

Now think back over the pace of the day. Was there a stretch where the heart ran ahead of the body? Perhaps you went faster to keep up with someone, or to prove something, or because the morning was so fine. Perhaps you stayed behind when you might have walked on, and felt a small, odd shame. Neither is a failure. Both are only information.

Whom did you listen to today? Perhaps someone said something sensible and you nodded and ignored it. Perhaps no one said anything, and you wished they had. There is nearly always someone nearby who has walked this road before, and most of them like to be asked.

Look at tomorrow's stage with the same honesty. The sensible distance is the one you could manage on a bad day, not the one you managed on a good one. If there is a shorter place to stop, know where it is. And do not measure yourself against the strongest person in the room. They have their own feet to answer to.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: Where did my enthusiasm run ahead of my body today?
Whose advice did I hear, and what would it be wise to do about it?
If tomorrow's walk had to be a little shorter than I planned, what would I gain?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Tired is not the same as hurt. Tiredness is the ordinary price of a good day, and it will mostly be gone by morning. But be honest with yourself about the difference. If you are not sure which of the two this is, treat it as the more careful one until you find out. A rest day is not a loss. Many people on long roads say that their best days came after they stopped trying to be strong.
A short prayer

Teach me the size of my own strength, and let me not be ashamed of it. Where I ran ahead today, forgive me, and let my body forgive me too. Give me patience to go a little slower, and the sense to listen to someone who knows. Let my feet rest tonight, and mend. Let the one who walks faster walk well, and the one who walks slower, and me.
What do you do when the high road is closed?
The passage

paras.t: So long as thou wearest a mortal body, thou shalt feel weariness and heaviness of heart. … At such a time it is expedient for thee to flee to humble and external works, and to renew thyself with good actions; to wait for My coming and heavenly visitation with sure confidence; to bear thy exile and drought of mind with patience, until thou be visited by Me again, and be freed from all anxieties. For I will cause thee to forget thy labours, and altogether to enjoy eternal peace.

spans.t: Reflection

Sooner or later, usually in the first week, there comes an afternoon on which nothing is wrong and everything is heavy. The road is straight. The sun is where it was an hour ago. You are not in pain, exactly, but you are used up, and the thoughts that carried you along on the first morning, the sense of purpose, the feeling that this was a good thing to be doing, have gone somewhere you cannot follow. You keep walking because stopping is not an option. It is not a crisis. It is just flat.

Thomas à Kempis knew this afternoon. In this chapter the voice that speaks to the reader is, in his telling, God's, and it begins with something every walker will recognise: you will not always be able to stay in the high clear air. A person cannot live permanently on the mountain. Weariness and heaviness of heart come with having a body, he says, and for as long as you have one, you will feel them.

What he suggests is almost comically modest. When the high road is closed, go down to the low one. Turn to humble and outward works, to small good actions, and renew yourself with those. Do not wait for the great feeling to return. Do something useful with your hands.

Anyone who has walked for a week has met this cure without knowing its name. Wash your socks. Hang them on the line. Sweep the floor where you slept. Peel the potatoes in the shared kitchen, or wash the pan someone else cooked in. Refill the bottle of the person whose hands are full. Mend the strap you have been meaning to mend. After half an hour of that, the heaviness has often lifted a little, not because the work was important, but because it was real, and small enough to finish. A mind that is dry does not need to be fed with big thoughts. It needs a task it can actually complete. Thomas spent much of his own life copying manuscripts by hand, and he knew how careful, repetitive work can steady a restless mind.

There is something else in the passage worth noticing: "good actions" are not only for the tidy. Kindness is one of them. A small, practical act for somebody else is a very good remedy for the flat afternoon, because it moves the attention off the weary self and onto something that needs doing now. This is not a trick. It is how people so often get through long days: by being useful to each other.

Then Thomas says the thing that gives the passage its patience. Wait, with confidence, until the lightness returns. Bear this dryness of mind, this "drought", he calls it, until you are visited again. That is a picture of the weather of a long walk. There are days when the legs seem not to belong to you, and then, quite without warning, a morning when they come back. It does not always happen on the day you want. But it happens often enough that it becomes a kind of trust.

Where is it hard? In two places. First, the passage promises that you will forget your labours and enjoy a perfect peace. That is a promise about the end, not the afternoon, and Thomas does not pretend otherwise. It may console you or it may sound far away. Both are fair. Second, and more important: ordinary tiredness and something deeper can look alike. Chores will not cure a real depression, and Thomas is not suggesting that they will. If the heaviness does not lift after a few days, or if it frightens you, say so to someone, a friend, a doctor, a person you trust. That is not weakness. It is exactly the kind of humble, practical action the passage is about.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? That when you are low, you reach for the nearest small honest task, and do it well, and do not demand more of yourself than that. An afternoon spent washing a shirt properly is not a wasted afternoon. It may be the thing that gets you to tomorrow.
For the walk

items.t: What is the smallest useful thing I can do right now, for myself or for someone near me? A small act for someone else counts as well: a held gate, a shared orange, a plaster for a stranger's heel.

When you next feel flat, do one task slowly and completely: wipe down your boots, fill your water bottle and someone else's, tidy the corner where your things are. Let your attention rest on your hands, and when you have finished, notice how you feel.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Your hands smell of soap, or of boot polish, or of the orange you peeled at four o'clock. There is a line of washing somewhere with a few small, ridiculous items on it, drying in whatever evening light is left. It is a humble sight, and a faintly cheering one.

Think back over the day, and ask a plain question: when was it heavy? Perhaps at some point in the afternoon the way you felt turned grey, and you could not say why. Perhaps it was a sudden dip after a good morning. Perhaps it was more like a low hum than a mood, and you only noticed it when it stopped. Do not try to explain it. Just see where it sat in the day.

And did it lift, at any point, even a little? If so, what had you been doing? Sometimes it is something very small: a conversation that had nothing to do with anything, a job with a beginning and an end, a shower. You may not have thought of it as a cure. It may well have been one.

If you did a small kindness today, however trivial, hold it for a moment. It need not have been noticed. If you received one, hold that too. The small economy of favours on this road is one of its great consolations, and it runs on very little.

Take a moment to notice what the small tasks did for you. Work with the hands has a way of making the mind better company. It is worth remembering this, because the next flat afternoon will not announce itself either.

And if there was a long grey patch today that nothing lifted, give that a plain note too. Not that you failed, only that some afternoons are stubborn. Say it to yourself in one line, so that tomorrow you can tell whether it was a day or the start of a pattern.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: When did the heaviness lift today, even slightly, and what was I doing?
What small, finishable thing could I do tomorrow when it comes back?
If it does not lift, who is the person I would tell?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. A tired body makes everything seem worse than it is, and at night the worst is the loudest. Nothing you decide at ten in the evening is final. If the day felt flat, that is allowed. A flat day is still a day walked, and flatness is something that passes, usually faster than expected, and often during sleep. You do not have to be cheerful about it. You only have to let the night do its part.
A short prayer

For the work that was small and honest today, thank you. For the weariness, let it ease in the dark. Let the lightness come back when it will, and let me not be afraid in the meantime. Let me be glad of small things. If someone needs a hand tomorrow, let me see them, and if I need one, let me ask.
Can you stop, and let stopping be enough?
The passage

paras.t: Grant unto me, above all things that I can desire, to rest in Thee, and that in Thee my heart may be at peace. Thou art the true peace of the heart, Thou alone its rest; apart from Thee all things are hard and unquiet. In Thee alone, the supreme and eternal God,
I will lay me down in peace and take my rest

spans.t: Reflection

The first rest day is stranger than it sounds. After a week of walking the body asks for it, and you give it a day, and the day arrives, empty and slow. You wake without an alarm. You do not need to be anywhere. The town goes on with its ordinary day as if you were not there, and you sit with a coffee and discover a sensation you had forgotten: you do not know what to do with your hands.

Many people find resting harder than walking. Walking has a purpose built into it. Rest has none, and into the gap come all the usual visitors: guilt, restlessness, the arithmetic of kilometres lost, the quiet suspicion that you ought to be improving yourself. It is common to fill a rest day with chores and errands and to reach the evening more tired than a walking day would have left you.

The passage is a prayer, the disciple's answer to the voice that has been speaking to him in his book. It asks for one thing above everything he can desire: to rest. And it says where. Not in a place, and not in an achievement, but in God, whom he calls the true peace of the heart, its only rest. Apart from that, he says, all things are hard and unquiet. The last words are borrowed from a psalm, and in the psalm they are about lying down to sleep.

A reader who does not pray as Thomas did may still hear what is going on underneath. He is saying that rest is not only a matter of the body. You can lie in the best bed in Spain and not rest. You can sit in a plain church for ten minutes and be quieter inside than you have been all month. The body can be helped by sleep and soup, and they are good things, but the part of us that keeps running after the body has stopped needs a different kind of place.

There is a hard side to that. "Apart from Thee all things are hard and unquiet" is a large claim, and not every reader will accept it as stated. Some find peace in a landscape, a friend, a quiet routine, work well done. Thomas does not forbid those. He is talking about a deeper layer, and he is sure it needs God. We can leave that as it is. Each reader will know whether it fits.

Often the mind, given nothing to do, begins to review the whole week at speed: every conversation, every small mistake. Let it, if it will, but ask it to be kind. A rest day is a poor time for a trial.

There is also a more ordinary difficulty. Rest is a skill, and it can be out of practice. Nobody mentions this on the first day of a long walk, when everyone is thinking about distance and pace. By the seventh day you learn that stopping takes some learning too. You have to stop doing the things that feel like progress: counting, planning, checking the next stage. You have to let a slow hour be slow.

It also happens that the first rest is not chosen. An injury, a storm, a closed bridge, a body that simply says no. If that is how the day has come to you, the passage has something kind to say. A place to rest is not a reward for walking. It is part of the walk, and it was always going to be needed.

Many traditions set aside one day in seven for stopping, and it was never meant as an indulgence. It was meant as a way of staying human. A pilgrim who cannot stop is only a very determined traveller.

What does it ask of an ordinary day, then? That for a few hours you do less than you planned. That you let a meal take an hour. That you sit on a bench with nothing in your hands and see what the restlessness does when it is not fed. It rises, it peaks, and, if you wait, it falls. Somewhere beyond it there is a quiet that was waiting to be noticed.
For the walk

items.t: When did I last stop without something to do next, and what did it feel like?

Sit for five minutes today with nothing in your hands: no phone, no map, no book. Watch the urge to do something rise and fall like a wave. When it has passed, stay one minute longer. If sitting is hard, count ten slow breaths and begin again.

spans.t: At the end of the day

One week. Seven mornings of boots and straps, and tonight there are no boots on the floor, because for once they have not been used. You may find that the evening of a rest day has a different quality from the others. It is softer, and a little slower. You are tired in a new way: not from distance, but from stopping.

Look back over the day, as you have been learning to. How did it go? Be honest: was it rest, or was it restlessness in a different place? Perhaps you spent the morning at the washing line, and the afternoon looking up the next stages on your phone. Perhaps you slept more than you thought you could. Perhaps there was a moment, in a church or on a bench or in a bath, when everything simply went quiet. If there was, hold it. If there was not, this is also normal. It sometimes takes the second rest day to learn how to have the first.

And since it is the seventh evening, you might glance back at the whole week as well. Not to judge it. Only to see it, the way you might look back along a road from a rise: how far you came, which bends you do not remember, what was harder than you thought, and what was easier. Notice, too, who you have met, and which faces you would be glad to see again.
After a rest day it is tempting to plan: tomorrow's stage, how to make up for the lost time. Leave that for the morning. A day of rest has not cost you a day.

If you spent part of today in a church or some other quiet corner, notice what you did there. Not what you should have done. Some people sit and say nothing at all. Some light a candle. Some simply look at the ceiling for a long while. All of that is rest, and all of it counts.
Three small questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I let go of today that I would usually have clung to?
When, if at all, did I feel properly rested, and where was I?
What do I want to carry from this week into the next one, and what can stay behind?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. A rest day can bring a tiredness of its own, the kind that arrives when the body relaxes and tells you the real total. If you are more tired tonight than you were last night, that is not a sign that the day failed. It means the body has finally been given room to say what it has been holding. Let it say it, and sleep. If sleep does not come at once, that is common after a rest day: the body has been quiet all afternoon and has less to ask of the night. Lie still, unclench your hands and your jaw, and let the thoughts go by like traffic. You are resting even when you are awake.
A short prayer

I have walked, and now I have stopped, and both were good. Let this bed be enough. Let the town sleep, and let me sleep with it. Whatever I have been running after, let it wait until morning. Give my body its rest and my heart its quiet, and let me wake ready for the road. Let the week behind me be a gift and not a debt.
Who is carrying something for you, and what are you carrying for them?
The passage

paras.t: Endeavour to be patient in bearing with other men’s faults and infirmities whatsoever they be, for thou thyself also hast many things which have need to be borne with by others. … But now hath God thus ordained, that we may learn to bear one another’s burdens, because none is without defect, none without a burden, none sufficient of himself, none wise enough of himself; but it behoveth us to bear with one another, to comfort one another, to help, instruct, admonish one another. How much strength each man hath is best proved by occasions of adversity: for such occasions do not make a man frail, but show of what temper he is.

spans.t: Reflection

Half past five in a dormitory is a good place to learn about people. Somewhere in the dark a plastic bag is being unpacked, one rustle at a time, by someone who has clearly decided that if they go slowly enough it will not count. Across the room there is a head torch, which sweeps your face as it passes. Beneath you, or above you, there is a man who has been snoring since ten in a steady, patient, thoroughly committed way. You lie there composing remarks.
Then, if you are lucky, you remember the sentence that Thomas à Kempis put at the front of this passage:
thou thyself also hast many things which have need to be borne with by others.

Somebody in this room, some night, has lain awake because of you. It may be the cough you do not notice, the zip, the late phone call, the boots. We rarely see ourselves as the irritant. Everyone else is the difficult one. Thomas, with his usual unflattering clarity, turns the sentence round.

The second half of the passage goes deeper. We are meant, he says, to learn to carry one another's burdens, because nobody is without a fault, nobody without a weight, nobody sufficient or wise enough alone. He lists what we owe each other: to bear with, to comfort, to help, to instruct, to correct. It is a small catalogue of what a community does, and a road is a kind of temporary community. The pilgrims who share a table tonight may never meet again, and yet for an evening they act like a family. Plasters pass from hand to hand. A charger is lent. Somebody mentions that the next stretch is longer than the sign suggests, and somebody else is glad to know. Water is shared. It happens so often that it is easy to forget it is a form of the thing Thomas is describing.

Then comes a line that deserves to be read slowly. Adversity, he says, does not make a person frail but shows what sort of person they are. Anyone who has watched other walkers in the rain will know how true that is. Tired, hungry, wet and late, people stop performing. Some turn out to be extraordinarily kind. Some discover a short temper they did not know they had. And you, in the same weather, will find out the same about yourself, sometimes with a small surprise.

There are two places where this passage is hard. The first is the idea of bearing with other people, which has a shadow side. Patience is a virtue when it takes a snorer's night on the chin. It is not a virtue when it puts up with something that is actually harmful: a person who makes you unsafe, who frightens you, who will not stop. Thomas is speaking of ordinary faults and infirmities, the everyday friction of people living close together. For anything beyond that, say so, and say it to the host or to someone you trust. Bearing with does not mean staying silent about harm.

The second hard place is the phrase "none sufficient of himself". Pride of self-sufficiency is a very common thing on the road. Some walkers insist on carrying every burden alone, refusing a lift, refusing a plaster, refusing a word of advice. It looks like strength. It is often a kind of loneliness. To receive help is a good deal harder than to give it, and the passage quietly asks you to do both.

And there is a plain, honest doubt. Some days you do not like people. You do not want to bear with them, comfort them or admonish them. You want to be left alone with your bread and your map. The passage does not demand that you like anybody. It only suggests that you will need to be borne with yourself, soon, and that a small courtesy given today will be useful credit tomorrow.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Two small things. To let one irritation go by without remark. And, once, to give or ask for a bit of help: a spare minute, a bit of tape, a seat made room for, a hand with a strap.
For the walk

items.t: Whose faults am I carrying today, and who is carrying mine? If you can, think of one person by name, and let your thoughts about them soften a little.

Do one small kindness before the next stop, and ask for one small kindness in return: directions, a moment's company, a spare hand. Take it with thanks, and notice how the day feels when you have both given and received. If that feels too much, simply greet someone you would normally walk past.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The long table in the shared kitchen is a place where the day is gathered up. Someone has made too much pasta and is offering it round. Someone is peeling an orange with great concentration. In three languages, nobody quite understands what anybody else is saying, and the conversation goes on perfectly well.

Think back over the people you met today. Some you will not remember by next week. Some will stay with you a long time, for no reason you could easily explain. Was there someone who was hard to bear? It may be the person from the early morning, with the bag, or someone in the afternoon who talked too much, or too little. Is there another way to see them? Perhaps they were frightened, or tired, or lonely, or hurting in a way that you could not see. You do not need to forgive anything tonight, only to loosen your grip a little.

And was there anyone who bore with you? It is worth noticing, because it often happens without a word. A person who gave up the lower bunk. Someone who let you pass on a narrow path, or waited while you found your map. A host who said nothing about the time. Our own faults are carried by other people far more often than we know.
If you gave help, however small, hold on to it for a moment, and let it be a small gladness. If you received help and found it hard to take, notice that too.

The last word on Thomas's list, to correct, is the delicate one. On a road where nobody has any standing, it usually means the gentlest sort of honesty: telling a friend that their pace is hurting them, or that their silence is worrying you. If there is someone like that, you might think tonight about whether a word is owed, and how kindly it could be said.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: Whose patience did I use today without noticing?
Who did I find hard to bear, and what might they be carrying that I cannot see?
What small help could I offer, or ask for, tomorrow?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Patience is the first thing to go when you are tired. The person who snapped at five o'clock was not the person you would like to be, but they were tired, and so was everyone else in the room. Do not judge the whole of yourself by the six o'clock version. You can begin again with the people in the morning, when everyone is a little kinder, a little more rested, and a little more ready to be borne with. Many a night's grievance has dissolved over the first coffee.
A short prayer

For the people who carried me today without saying so, thank you. For the ones I found hard, let me see them more gently. Forgive my own noise and my own faults, and let them be lightly borne. Let me be glad to help, and not ashamed to ask. Let those who snore be forgiven, and those who lie awake be patient. Let this room sleep in peace.
What would you do today if you knew how the walk ends?
The passage

paras.t: A certain man being in anxiety of mind, continually tossed about between hope and fear, and being on a certain day overwhelmed with grief, cast himself down in prayer before the altar in a church, and meditated within himself, saying, “Oh! if I but knew that I should still persevere,” and presently heard within him a voice from God, “And if thou didst know it, what wouldst thou do? Do now what thou wouldst do then, and thou shalt be very secure.” And straightway being comforted and strengthened, he committed himself to the will of God and the perturbation of spirit ceased, neither had he a mind any more to search curiously to know what should befall him hereafter, but studied rather to inquire what was the good and acceptable will of God, for the beginning and perfecting of every good work.

spans.t: Reflection

Somewhere in the second week the question arrives, and it rarely arrives at a good moment. It comes on a long uphill, or in the last hour before a stop, or at two in the morning in a strange bed. Will I finish? Will the knee hold? What if the blister turns into something? What if I get there and nothing has changed? What if I stop and everyone knows I stopped? The questions are not stupid. They are only unanswerable, and they are very good at keeping you awake.

Thomas à Kempis tells a short story about a man in this position. It is a story he tells without naming anyone. The man is anxious, tossed between hope and fear, overwhelmed with grief, and one day he falls to his knees in a church and says, in effect, what many of us have said in our own way:
If I only knew that I should still persevere.
If I only knew I would make it.
The answer he receives is short, and it is a question.
And if thou didst know it, what wouldst thou do?
The man does not have to think very long. He would keep going. He would do whatever he is already trying to do, with a little less fear. And so the voice says:
Do now what thou wouldst do then, and thou shalt be very secure.

It is worth turning that over slowly, because it is cleverer than it first appears. The man wants a guarantee before he acts. But a guarantee would not change what he did today. It would only change how he felt while he did it. So the thing he is waiting for is not what he needs. What he needs is already in his hands: the next step, the next act, the next honest effort. If you would walk on knowing you would arrive, then walk on, and let the knowing go. Today's task is the same either way.

Then the story ends with a small, beautiful sentence. The man's disturbance of spirit ceased, and he no longer wanted to search into what would happen to him in the future. He wanted, instead, to ask what the good thing to do was, now. The question changes from
what will happen
to
what is the right thing to do next
. That is a much smaller question, and a much easier one to answer.

For a walker it translates cleanly. You cannot know whether your knee will last, or whether you will reach the cathedral. You can know whether to drink water now, to stop at the next village, to take the shorter path, to ask a pharmacist about that tendon. The big question is out of reach. The small ones are all within your hands, and they are the ones that decide the big one.

Where is it hard? The passage works best on one kind of doubt, the kind that is about getting through. It is much less helpful on a different kind, the doubt about why you are walking at all. A man who asks "Is this worth doing?" is not answered by "Keep going". For that question there may be no tidy reply. You may walk for days with it unresolved, and the passage does not pretend to settle it. What it may do is suggest that the question can be carried while you walk, and need not be answered before the next step.

There is another difficulty. The man in the story receives an answer, a voice, in a church. Many people never do. They kneel, or sit, or walk, and hear only the wind. Thomas does not say this is a failure. He tells the story because it happened to someone, and offers it as a possibility, not a promise. Whether or not you expect a voice, the question it asked is a good one to carry by yourself.
What does it ask of an ordinary day? Each time an "if only" comes up, finish the sentence honestly:
and so today I will...
The knee, the distance, the cathedral and the verdict of other people can wait. Today's walk is enough to be getting on with.
For the walk

items.t: If I knew for certain how this walk will end, what would I do differently today? Answer honestly. Nobody will hear.

Each time a "what if" rises in your mind, answer it with "and so, now, I will...", and name one small thing within reach: a sip of water, the next waymark, a greeting. Do that thing, and let the "what if" stand where it is. If the worry is large, make the small thing smaller: only the next ten steps.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If you are lying awake with the questions, you are in good company. Doubt keeps late hours, and it is at its most persuasive between eleven and three. It is worth remembering that nothing you think in the dark has a vote in the morning. Let the thoughts come, and let them be heard, and then, if you can, put them down.

Look back over the day with the story in mind. Where did "if only" visit you? Perhaps it was on a climb, or at the point where the path divided. Perhaps it came while you were waiting for something: a bed, an answer, a message. Perhaps it lived somewhere in the background all day like a radio in another room. Name the biggest "if" of the day. Say it plainly, once, in a whisper or in a single line on paper. A worry that has been named has edges, and a worry that is only carried has none.

Then ask a second question: what did you do anyway? There is nearly always something. You walked the hill with the "if" in your head. You asked about the path. You drank water, ate bread, and stepped over the next stone. That, the passage says, is the whole business: you did, now, what you would have done then. It is more than it sounds.

And if the big doubt, the "why am I doing this at all", was also with you today, it can stay unsettled tonight. Nobody has to resolve it in a bunk. Some people carry it for the whole walk and understand only afterwards what it was for. Some people never do, and walk well all the same.

There is one more thing worth seeing. Many of the people in this room have the same questions in their heads tonight, and are as quiet about them as you are. A walker's reserve can hide a great deal of the same fear. Tomorrow, an honest word to someone might lighten the load for both of you.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What was the biggest "if" of today, and what did I do in spite of it?
Is there a smaller, answerable question hiding inside the large, unanswerable one?
What is one thing I can do tomorrow without knowing how it ends?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Doubt and exhaustion look very alike from the inside, and they often travel together. A worry that sounded like a verdict at midnight may sound much more like a worry after breakfast. If it is still there in the morning, with food inside you, take it seriously then. Tonight, the most useful thing is to lie still and let sleep be the answer for now.
A short prayer

I do not know how this ends, and tonight I will not try to find out. Let me do what is in front of me, and do it without fear. Quiet the questions that have no answers yet. Let me rest in the small certainty that I walked today, and that tomorrow there will be a next step.

chapters.title: Day 10. He doth much who loveth much

spans.t: What are you counting, and who are you counting it for?
The passage

paras.t: Without charity no work profiteth, but whatsoever is done in charity, however small and of no reputation it be, bringeth forth good fruit; for God verily considereth what a man is able to do, more than the greatness of what he doth. … He doth much who loveth much. He doth much who doth well. … He envieth none, because he longeth for no selfish joy; nor doth he desire to rejoice in himself, but longeth to be blessed in God as the highest good.

spans.t: Reflection

"How far did you walk today?" It is the standard question on a long road, and everyone asks it, usually before asking a name. The answer is a number, and the number does a surprising amount of work. It places you. It tells the other person whether you are ahead or behind, strong or cautious, keen or sensible. Most of us have felt it, that small flicker of pleasure at a large figure, and that small flinch at a modest one. Phones help. They keep count of steps, hours, climbs, and offer a tidy summary at the end of the day.

There is nothing wrong with numbers. You need some of them to plan a stage, to book a bed, to work out the water. The trouble starts when they turn into a ranking. Then they stop being information and become a verdict, and everyone on the road is quietly marked out of ten.

Thomas à Kempis, who never carried a phone, had a different yardstick, and it is worth reading carefully. He says that any work done in love, however small and unnoticed, bears good fruit, and that God, as he puts it, considers what a person is able to do, more than the greatness of what they do. The measure is not the size of the deed. It is the size of the deed against what you had to give.

That changes the arithmetic. A tired person who walks twelve kilometres on a day when twelve is all there is has done more, in this reckoning, than a strong person who walks thirty on a day when thirty was easy. The one who gives up a seat, or waits for a slower friend, or says a kind thing at the end of a bad day, may have done a great deal, even if it appears nowhere on any screen.
Then come two short sentences that seem almost too simple.
He doth much who loveth much. He doth much who doth well.

The first puts love ahead of quantity. The second puts care ahead of speed. One way to read them together is as a practical test: not how much, but how lovingly and how well. Anyone who has watched a person bandage a blister with real attention, or fill a stranger's bottle without being asked, will know what is being measured.

In the passage's last sentence the effect appears. A person who loves in this way, he says, envies nobody, because they long for no selfish joy. Envy is the shadow of ranking. As soon as you stop trying to win, there is no one left to envy. The strong walker ahead of you is not your competitor. They are someone with a different body and a different road.

Here the passage is hard in two places. First, "of no reputation" is a demanding phrase. Almost everyone wants to be seen doing well, and it is odd, and a little painful, to be asked to do something good that no one will ever notice. The old advice to do small things well in secret runs against the grain of a world of photographs and totals. Second, "he doth well" has a perfectionist's shadow. It does not mean that you must do everything flawlessly or not at all. A blister dressed clumsily and kindly is still a kindness.

There is also a plain doubt. Numbers are comforting. They give a day a shape. To walk without them, even for an hour, can feel like losing a handrail. That is a fair feeling, and it is no failure of character. The passage does not ask you to burn your pedometer. It asks only that you notice what is being measured, and by whom, and whether the measure is yours.

"Charity", in Thomas's old English, means love, not donations. It is the thing that gives a small act its weight. If you want a one-line version of the whole passage, it might be this: your effort is measured against your own capacity, and that is the only fair scale.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? That for a stretch you walk without counting, and ask yourself only whether you are walking well. And that you do one small good thing today, without telling anyone.
For the walk

items.t: What am I counting today, and who am I counting it for? Ask it without judging the answer.
