For one hour, do not look at the distance, the time or the steps. Ask only, every so often, "Am I walking well?" And do one small good thing quietly, so that nobody notices, and leave it unmentioned. If you catch yourself composing tonight's number in your head, smile at it and let it go.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The evening begins, as it always does, with a question that is also a number. "How far today?" You may have heard it two or three times already, over the washing up, across the table, in the queue for the shower. Think about how it felt to answer. Did you hear yourself adjusting the figure, rounding it up, saying it a little too lightly? Did you feel better or worse once you had heard someone else's?

Look back over the day with the passage's yardstick in your hand, which is capacity and not size. What did you do today that was large for you? It may have been nothing that would sound impressive: a hill taken slowly, a hard stretch finished, a conversation you were afraid to have. Give it its proper weight. Be fair to yourself on the scale that counts.

What did you do that no one saw? If you did something small and kind today, and it passed without a word, hold it for a moment. It is the kind of thing the passage means. If you cannot think of anything, you may have done several without noticing. Most of what is done in love goes unrecorded, including by the person who did it.

And was there anyone you envied? It is a very human thing, and it appears with surprising force on long walks. It may have been someone faster, or lighter, or quieter, or simply someone who seemed to be enjoying it more. Name what you wanted from them. It is often something other than what you first thought, and it may be something you can find for yourself.

If you did walk far today, you do not need to apologise for it. If you walked little, you do not need to explain. The passage cuts both ways. And there is a gentler number to end on, if you want one: the number of people who were kind to you today. It is often larger than the distance feels.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I count today, and did counting help me or hurt me?
What did I do today that nobody saw, and does it matter to me that nobody did?
Whom did I envy, and what did they have that I actually wanted?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Comparing is worst when you are tired. At the end of a hard day, the walker who looks fresh and tells you cheerfully how far they went can seem like a rebuke. They are not. They are another person with another body and another history. The stage you walked is the stage you walked, and it was enough. Let the numbers go quiet for the night, and let the day be only what it was.
A short prayer

For the small things done today that nobody counted, thank you. Let me be satisfied with what I was able to give. Take the measuring tape out of my hands tonight. Where I envied, let me wish well. Where I was proud, let me smile at it. Let love be my measure, and let it be enough. Let me sleep without being ranked.
What if the bad day is not the whole story?
The passage

paras.t: What doth care about future events bring thee, save sorrow upon sorrow? Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. … It is vain and useless to be disturbed or lifted up about future things which perhaps will never come. … When thou thinkest thyself far removed from Me, I am often the nearer. When thou reckonest that almost all is lost, then often is greater opportunity of gain at hand. All is not lost when something goeth contrary to thy wishes.

spans.t: Reflection

Some days go wrong in a row. A wrong turn, then a long road in the rain, then a village with its one café shut, then the news that the bed you were counting on is not there. By four o'clock the mind has stopped dealing with the day and begun to deal with the future. If this is how it is today, how will it be tomorrow? If the plan has failed once, why will it work later? You start rehearsing disasters that have not happened, with great skill and in considerable detail.

Thomas à Kempis knew the habit, and this passage is aimed at it. In this chapter the voice that speaks to the reader is, in his telling, God's, answering a person in trouble. And what it says is practical. What does worry about the future bring you, it asks, except sorrow upon sorrow? Then it quotes a line from the Gospel of Matthew, in the old translation:
Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof.
Each day has enough of its own. Do not borrow tomorrow's.

Next it says that it is vain and useless to be disturbed about future things that may never come. The word "perhaps" is doing important work. Most of the disasters we rehearse on a bad afternoon never turn up. The rain stops. The next village has a bed. The blister is tended, and heals. The mind, after all, is very bad at forecasting.

Then comes the line that gives the passage its warmth. When you think you are far from help, it says, help is often nearer. When you reckon that almost everything is lost, there is often a better chance of gain at hand. And then, quietly: nothing is lost just because something has gone against what you wished.

There is a great deal of ordinary road experience in this. Walkers tell stories, and tell them often, of the day that went wrong and turned out to be the one they remember. The wrong turn that led through a village they would never have seen. The closed door that led to a parish hall, a kind stranger, a pot of soup. Thomas is not promising that this always happens. He says "often", and it is a careful word. But the shape is familiar, and it is worth remembering at four o'clock.

Where is it hard? The passage is easily misread as "everything will work out", and that is not a promise anyone can honestly make. Some losses are real. A death, an injury that ends the walk, a job gone, a friendship broken: none of these is answered by "all is not lost". The sentence here is about something smaller: a day, a plan, a wish that went contrary. It does not say that nothing has been lost. It says that not everything has. In the case of a great loss this book has less to offer, and it says so plainly. A person carrying that should have other people close, and good help.

There is a second difficulty. The passage speaks of feeling far from help, and it hints that feeling is not the same as fact. That is true, and it is also hard to hear. When you are cold and hungry and discouraged, the feeling of being alone is as convincing as any fact. All Thomas suggests is that you hold it a little more loosely, and do not treat today's mood as tomorrow's forecast.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? That at the worst moment you stop, and look around, and count what is still intact. Legs, a little water, some bread, the road ahead, a day that will end. That you leave tomorrow to tomorrow. And that, when the plan collapses, you wait a minute before you decide what the collapse means. The first reading of a bad moment is rarely the right one.

You do not need to feel consoled. You only need to let the door stay slightly open for something unexpected. It sometimes comes in the shape of a person, and sometimes in the shape of a bench. Sometimes it is just the next kilometre turning out to be easier than the last.
For the walk

items.t: What have I decided is lost today that may only be delayed or changed? Be as specific as you can.

At the next moment when something goes wrong, stop for two minutes before you react. Look around and name three things that are still all right: your legs, a bit of water, the light. Then decide what to do next. If you cannot find three, find one, and look at it properly.

spans.t: At the end of the day

You are in the place you ended up, which may or may not be the place you meant to be. Whatever the plan was this morning, it has been revised, cancelled, replaced, or has quietly turned out to have been fine all along. The bed is a bed. The ceiling is a ceiling. You are indoors, and you are fed, or soon will be.

Think back over what went against you today. It might have been large or small: a wrong turn, a closed door, rain, a conversation that went badly, a shoe that rubbed. Take them one at a time, and ask what each one turned out to be. Did the wrong turn cost you an hour or give you something? Was the closed café the end of a plan or the start of another? Some of them will have been simply bad, with nothing hidden in them. Let them be that, without making a lesson of it. Not every setback is secretly a gift.

But look, too, for anything that came at the edge of the trouble. A person who turned up. A decision made for you that you were glad of afterwards. A moment of unexpected kindness at the lowest point of the afternoon. If there was one, it is worth saying thank you for it, silently or aloud.

Then the future, which has probably been knocking at the door all evening. Tomorrow's weather. Tomorrow's distance. Tomorrow's bed. Leave it outside. It will still be there in the morning, and it will be easier to deal with when you are fed and rested. Tonight's work is only to put the day down.

A small ritual for the end of a day like this: say, or write, three things that went right, however trivial. A hot shower. A dry pair of socks. A kind word. It is not that the bad things did not happen. It is that the mind tends to keep only one side of the ledger, and tonight you can put in the other.
If someone near you has had a worse day than yours, a word costs very little.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What went against my wishes today, and what did it actually turn out to be?
What am I afraid of tomorrow that may never come?
What was still intact today that I forgot to count?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. The mind that is tired is a catastrophist. It reads every small thing as a sign and every sign as a warning. If tonight everything seems to be going wrong, remember that you are judging the whole of the road from the lowest point of a long day. Eat, wash, lie down. The sentence about "all is not lost" can wait for you until you are rested enough to believe it.
A short prayer

Let me put down the day's worries here. Whatever went wrong, let it be over. Whatever I fear for tomorrow, let it wait until morning. Be near me where I thought I was alone. Let me close this day gently. Let me sleep, knowing that not everything is lost, and that something good may already be on its way.

chapters.title: Day 12. A little puff of wind

spans.t: Why does the small thing undo us?
The passage

paras.t: I will confess to Thee, Lord, my infirmity. It is often a small thing which casteth me down and maketh me sad. I resolve that I will act bravely, but when a little temptation cometh, immediately I am in a great strait. Wonderfully small sometimes is the matter whence a grievous temptation cometh, and whilst I imagine myself safe for a little space; when I am not considering, I find myself often almost overcome by a little puff of wind.

spans.t: Reflection

It is almost never the mountain. People cross high passes, endure a week of rain, walk on through a bad knee, and then lose their temper over a pebble. The pebble is in the boot, a very small hard thing, and it has been there for twenty minutes because stopping to deal with it would admit that the day was not going to plan. By the time you sit down on the verge, the pebble is the whole of the problem and the fault of everyone you have ever met.

Thomas à Kempis, writing as the disciple in his own third book, makes one of the most honest confessions in the whole Imitation. It is often, he says, a small thing that casts him down and makes him sad. He resolves to act bravely, and when a little temptation comes, immediately he is in a great strait. He imagines himself safe for a short while, and then, without noticing, he is almost overcome by a puff of wind.

A puff of wind. It is a lovely, humbling image. A strong man knocked sideways by a breeze. Anybody who has promised themselves a calm, patient, generous walk and then snapped at a stranger in a queue for the shower will know it. The resolutions were real, and so was the weakness. The wind needed only to be a little cold.

Notice two things in the passage. The first is that the matter is "wonderfully small". The trouble is usually not a great temptation but a trivial one: a remark, a delay, a smell, a sudden wish to stop. The second is the timing. He says that he was imagining himself safe, and was not considering, when the wind came. The dangerous moment is not in the middle of the struggle. It is just after a good stretch, when the guard is down. The arrival at the
albergue
after a fine day is often the very moment when something sharp is said.

"Temptation" is a heavy word, and in modern ears it can sound like a list of vices. A plainer way to read it is: anything that pulls you off your own intention. A taxi at the edge of the village. A shortcut along the road. A comment that begs for a clever reply. A decision to quit, made at four in the afternoon. Many of these are not wicked in themselves. Sometimes the taxi is the sensible thing, and to refuse it would be a kind of vanity. What Thomas is pointing at is the moment of being tugged, and the small gap in which you can choose.

Where is it hard? Perhaps in the tone. A confession of "my infirmity" can slide, in the hands of a person who is hard on himself, into self-contempt. Thomas is sometimes that person, and this book does not follow him there. The useful part of the passage is the honesty, not the shame. To say plainly "this is how I am knocked off course" is not a failure. It is the beginning of knowing where to put your guard.

There is also a plain honesty about the odds. The man in the passage resolves, falls, resolves again. He does not say that he has stopped falling. He says that this is what he is like, and he says it to the one he trusts most. That is a kind of wisdom: not to expect to become a person who is never moved by a breeze, but to become a person who notices sooner.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? A few small defences. Name the thing when it comes: "This is the puff of wind." A name takes some of the force out of it. Take three breaths before you answer or act. And deal with the actual pebble at once. Stop, sit down, take off the boot, shake it out. It takes thirty seconds, and it turns out to be a surprisingly good picture of the whole practice: do not walk on, out of stubbornness, with a small hard thing rubbing at you.
For the walk

items.t: What small thing is most likely to knock me off my course today, and what would a steadier answer look like?

Take three breaths before you react to the next small irritation, and if you can, name it silently: "puff of wind." And if there is a stone in your boot, literally or otherwise, stop and deal with it now, even though it costs a minute.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Tonight is a good time to be gentle with the person who walked today. Boots off. A cup of something warm. A moment, before you do anything else, in which nothing needs to be defended.

Think back for your puff of wind. Almost everyone had one. It may have been a sharp word, said or swallowed. It might have been a flash of envy, or a sudden decision to cut the day short. It might have been so small that you only noticed it afterwards: a slight meanness in the way you answered, a quick resentment over the last place in the queue. Do not be dramatic about it. Find it, look at it for a moment, and name it plainly.

What did you do next? That is the more interesting question, and it is often better than you fear. Perhaps you went on and stewed. Perhaps you recovered quickly and let it pass. Perhaps you apologised, or meant to. Whatever it was, you are not required to defend it tonight. And what would you have liked to do instead? A different word, a slower answer, a laugh? Holding the better version in mind, without scolding, is how it becomes easier next time.

If there is something that needs mending, an apology or a word of thanks, it can almost always wait for the morning, when you are rested and the other person is, too. Tired words made at night rarely repair anything.

Try also to remember where you were standing when it happened. Tired? Hungry? Too hot, or too cold? The pattern is often in the circumstances and not in the character, and knowing that gives you something practical to do about it, which is to eat, drink or sit down a little earlier.

And look for the places where you did not fall. A remark you let go by. A shortcut you declined. A sharp reply that you swallowed. These are easy to overlook, because nothing visibly happened, and they are exactly what the passage is hoping for.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What small thing knocked me off course today?
What did I do next, and what would I have liked to do?
What pause, word or habit could I put in place tomorrow to meet it better?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. The end of the day is exactly when the guard is lowest, and much of what we regret saying has been said tired. If you were short with someone this evening, it is quite likely that you were simply spent. That is not an excuse, only an explanation, and a reason to be kind to yourself. The point of the passage is not to make you ashamed of your weakness. It is to help you see it coming, and to give you an extra moment before the wind arrives.
A short prayer

Forgive the small unkindnesses of today, the ones I noticed and the ones I did not. Let the breeze that knocks me about be a little gentler tomorrow, and let me be a little steadier. Teach me to stop and shake out the stone. Where I fell, help me rise without shame. Let the wind drop tonight, and let the evening be calm. Now let me rest.
What is the smallest gift you have been given today?
The passage

paras.t: Be thankful, therefore, for the least benefit and thou shalt be worthy to receive greater. Let the least be unto thee even as the greatest, and let that which is of little account be unto thee as a special gift. If the majesty of the Giver be considered, nothing that is given shall seem small and of no worth, for that is not a small thing which is given by the Most High God.

spans.t: Reflection

On a long road you learn very quickly what is large and what is small, and then you learn that you had it the wrong way round. A glass of cold water, after four hours without, is not a small thing. Neither is a bench in the shade at the exact moment you need to sit. Or a hot shower after a cold day, or a tap in a village square. A sandwich pressed on you by a stranger. A shaded stretch of path when the sun has become personal. At home these things are scenery. Out here they change the weather inside you.

Thomas à Kempis noticed the same thing six centuries ago, and drew a sensible conclusion. Be thankful for the least benefit, he says, and let the least be to you as the greatest. Let what seems of little account be received as a special gift. This is not asking you to pretend. It is asking you to do the opposite of pretending: to look straight at a small thing and see how big it is.

There is a second thought folded into the passage. If the majesty of the Giver is considered, he says, nothing that is given can seem small. In his view all gifts come, in the end, from God, and so even a crust of bread carries weight. A reader who does not share that belief can still take the shape of it. Look at where the small gift came from. Somebody put out the jug. Somebody planted the fig tree by the wall. Somebody painted that yellow arrow, years ago or last month. Somebody built the bench. The smallness of the gift is only on the surface. Behind it there is often a person, or a long chain of them, who thought about you without knowing your name.
Walkers sometimes say that the small gifts seem to multiply the longer the road goes on. They do not multiply. The eyes have simply learned to count them.

There is a moment in the passage that sounds a little transactional: be thankful for little, and you will be worthy to receive more. It can read like a trade, with gratitude as the price. A kinder way to take it is as a description of capacity. People who cannot notice small things cannot take in large ones. A mind that is always reaching for the next thing has no room to receive what is already in its hand. Gratitude is partly a skill of attention, and it grows with use.

Where is it hard? There is a shadow on this subject, and honesty requires that it be named. "Be thankful" can be a cruel thing to say to someone who is in pain or loss. A few lines further on in the same chapter Thomas goes on to ask for thanks even for hardship, and this reading does not follow him there. Nobody should be told to be grateful for suffering. The passage we have here is about something much smaller and safer: noticing the good things that are actually good.

There is also the ordinary difficulty of attention. Most of the time, gratitude is simply not on the programme. The mind is on the next stage and the next meal. A person can go all day and be handed ten small gifts without noticing one. That is not a moral failing. It is only what happens to a mind that is busy.

And a plain doubt: some days you do not feel grateful, and no amount of looking will bring it on. If that is today, let it be. The practice is about noticing, not about producing a feeling. A feeling that has been forced is worth nothing. A gift noticed without much feeling is still a gift noticed.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? To catch the small gifts in the act. Before each stop, name three that you have been given in the last hour. The temperature of the air. A kind word. The ground, still there under your feet. And once, to say thank you to a person for something small, and to mean it with your whole face.
For the walk

items.t: What is the smallest thing I have been given today, and who or what stands behind it? Try to find something you would usually pass without noticing.

At each stop, name three small gifts of the last hour, silently or aloud. Before the end of the day, thank one person for one small thing, and let them see that you mean it. A plain "thank you" said slowly is enough.

spans.t: At the end of the day

It would be tempting at this hour to go through the day like an accounts clerk, making a list of things to be grateful for, and ticking them off with a sigh. Do not do that. Gratitude produced by obligation is stale. Instead, go slowly back over the day, as you might leaf through a photograph album, and see which small things come up on their own.

Perhaps it was the cold water. Perhaps a stranger's smile, or a stretch of path with a view you did not expect. Perhaps the plain fact of a mattress. Perhaps your own legs, which went on doing what you asked without being thanked, hour after hour. Aim for the very smallest things you can find. The point of the passage is the least, and the least is where most of the day's gifts actually live.

Then think about who stood behind them. Often it was someone you did not meet: whoever washed the sheets, cooked the soup, mended the path, kept the tap running. It is a strange and rather lovely thing to realise how many people have helped you today who will never know it. If there is a way, tomorrow, to pass something on to someone else, a small courtesy, a clean kitchen, a held gate, that is a kind of thank-you to them.
If there was a gift today that you did not notice at the time and see only now, say a word of thanks for that, too. It is not too late. Gifts can be received after the fact.

Here is a small exercise. Go through the day from morning to night and pick out the first gift and the last. The first may have been the coffee, or the quiet of the street. The last may be this very bed, or the sound of the room settling around you. Between them the day is full of others.
If you shared something today, food, water, a seat, a bit of tape, remember that giving is one way of saying thank you, and receiving gracefully is another.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What was the smallest gift of today?
Whom did I forget to thank?
What did I treat as small that was really large?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Gratitude is not a duty at ten o'clock at night. If you are too tired to feel anything, you do not have to produce anything. A single thing named is enough, however flat it feels. "The bed" is a perfectly good answer. And if the day was hard, and nothing seems to deserve thanks, you are allowed to leave the question open until tomorrow, when the light will come back and the small things with it.
A short prayer

Thank you for the water and the shade, for the bench, the bread, and the stranger's smile. Thank you for the people I will never meet who made this day easier. Let me notice more tomorrow, and be quicker to say so. Where I have nothing to say tonight, let silence do for thanks. Let me sleep, and be glad.
What can you say when the words run out?
The passage

paras.t: O Jesus, Light of Eternal Glory, solace of the wandering soul, before Thee my mouth is without speech, and my silence speaketh to Thee. How long will my Lord delay to come unto me? Let Him come unto me, His poor and humble one, and make me glad. … “Behold, here I am! Behold, I come to thee, for thou didst call Me. Thy tears and the longing of thy soul, thy humbleness and contrition of heart have inclined Me, and brought Me to thee.”

spans.t: Reflection

At the end of the second week there is often an afternoon with a door in it. It might be a church, left open for the hour, with a smell of old stone and candle wax and the cool that hits you as you step in from the heat. It might be a chapel by a crossing, or a stone wall in the shade with nobody about. You have no particular reason to go in. But the legs slow down, and you find that you are sitting, with the pack beside you, and that you have nothing at all to say.

That is the state this passage describes. The words in it are the disciple's, and they are among the most tender in the whole book. Before You, he says, my mouth is without speech, and my silence speaks to You. The title he gives to God is
solace of the wandering soul
, and it is hard for a walker to read it without a small start. A wandering soul. A solace for the one who is on the move and has not arrived.

His silence is not an absence of prayer. It is a form of it. Most people know this from the other side. Anybody who has sat with a friend in grief, or in the hospital, or in a car outside a house they cannot bring themselves to enter, has felt that some silences say more than anything that could be said aloud. They are full. They hold the whole of what is there, without making it smaller by explaining it.

Then, in the next sentence, the silence breaks, and what comes out is an honest complaint. How long will my Lord delay to come to me? It is the kind of question prayer is allowed to ask. It is impatient and hurt and a little sulky, and it comes from the same man whose silence we have just admired. The old books of prayer are full of such moments. They do not clean up the longing into something polite. They say: I have been waiting. Where are You?
And then, in the reply, the passage turns.
Behold, here I am.
The voice does not argue or explain. It says, I am here, because you called. Your tears and the longing of your soul have drawn me. It is a short, warm answer, and it comes at once.

Where is it hard? Perhaps here. In this book the answer comes within a few lines, and in life it often does not. A great many people sit in a quiet church, or on a wall, or in a bunk, and hear nothing. Some hear a great deal that is not comforting. Thomas knows this too, and a good deal of his book is about the long dry stretches. But in this chapter he offers the moment of answer as a possibility, and we can take it as one without insisting that it has to be ours.

There is a second hard thing. For a person in real grief, silence may be the only honest speech, and it may not feel like a solace at all. It may feel like a room with the furniture taken out. If that is where you are, nothing here asks you to fill it. You are not required to feel consoled, or to feel anything. To sit in the room, and let it be as empty as it is, is already a kind of answer to the question the passage asks.

And there is plain doubt. You may sit in the shade and wonder whether anyone is listening at all. That is a fair thing to wonder, and the passage does not scold you for it. The disciple is wondering too.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? A few minutes with no words. You do not need a church, though a church, where one is open, will often give you the quiet for nothing. Sit, with your hands open on your knees. Let whatever is there be there. If a word comes, let it be a small one.
For the walk

items.t: If I had no words at all, what would my silence say? Do not answer yet. Carry it.

Find a quiet place today, a church if there is one open, a wall in the shade if not, and sit for five minutes with your hands open on your knees. Say nothing. If a word comes, let it be a single small one: "here". When the five minutes are over, get up slowly.

spans.t: At the end of the day

You have reached the end of the second week, and the room is as it is. There may be a window, with the light going. There may be a few people already asleep, a few still talking quietly. Tonight, the day's last word may not need to be a word.

Look back at the day for its silences. Not the ones you chose, necessarily, but the ones that arrived. There may have been a long stretch of the morning when nobody spoke. There may have been a moment of stillness in a doorway or at a crossing, when something simply stopped. Perhaps you stood in front of a view and could not say what you felt. Perhaps you stood at a doorway and went on. Whatever these were, they were part of the day, and they may be the part that stays.

Then ask a harder question, if you are able to. What did you carry today that has no words? There is almost always something: a loss, a hope, a person, a question that has been with you since before you set out. It does not have to be named tonight. It can simply be held, as you might hold a stone in a pocket. The passage says that silence of this kind is not empty, and that it is heard.

If there is something you wish you could say to somebody, and have not, tonight is not too late to think about it, even if you cannot yet say it. Sometimes the first step is only to see that it is there.

Two weeks is the middle of things, whatever the length of your road. The first rush of newness has gone, and the end is not yet near enough to hurry you. Something has probably shifted in these fourteen days: the pace of your feet, the people you know by sight, the things you notice and the things you have stopped noticing. You do not have to measure the change tonight. It is enough to see that you are not the person who set out.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I carry today that had no words?
When was I most alone, and did it feel empty or full?
Is there something I would like to say to someone, even if I cannot say it yet?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. At night silence is not a discipline, only a mercy. If you are very tired, do not try to make the quiet mean something. Let the room be dark, let your breathing slow, and let the day end without comment. If it is true, as the passage says, that silence speaks, then you have already said all that was needed.
A short prayer

I have no words tonight, and I will not look for any. Whatever I carry, I set it down in the quiet. If anyone is listening, let them hear what I cannot say. If no one is, let the dark be gentle anyway. I am here. Let that be enough, and let tomorrow's road begin gently. Let the quiet last until morning, and keep me company in it.
Can you have peace without everything going right?
The passage

paras.t: My peace is with the humble and lowly in heart. Thy peace shall be in much patience. … Yet never to feel any disquiet, nor to suffer any pain of heart or body, this belongeth not to the present life, but is the state of eternal rest. Therefore count not thyself to have found true peace, if thou hast felt no grief; nor that then all is well if thou hast no adversary; nor that this is perfect if all things fall out according to thy desire.

spans.t: Reflection

There is a kind of evening that every walker remembers. The boots are off, the feet are up, a plastic cup of something cold is in your hand, and the light across the fields has gone the colour of honey. Nothing is wrong. You are clean, fed, a little sunburnt, and quite certain that this is the best place in the world to be. It is peace of a sort, and it is easy to take it for the real thing.

Then the light goes, someone starts a conversation that grates, you realise your sock has a hole, and the peace goes with it. It was peace of the kind that depends on conditions. It lasted exactly as long as everything was right.

Thomas à Kempis is talking about another kind. The chapter this passage comes from begins with the voice of Christ saying that his peace is not given the way the world gives it. Then it makes a plain, rather bracing claim. Peace, it says, is with the humble and the lowly in heart, and it grows in much patience.

The second part of the passage is the surprising one. To feel no disquiet at all, to suffer no pain of heart or body, is not something this life provides. That, he says, is the state of eternal rest. So you are not to think that you have found true peace because you have felt no grief. Nor that all is well because you have no adversary. Nor that things are perfect because everything has gone according to your wishes.

Read that again. It does not say that grief means peace has failed. It says that the absence of grief is not the same thing as peace. They are different things. A day with no trouble can be a day with no peace in it. And, by the same logic, a day with a lot of trouble can have a quiet place in the middle of it. Peace, in this reading, is not the absence of trouble. It is something that can sit alongside it, and does not need the trouble to leave before it arrives.

Walkers know something about this. The best moments are often not the most comfortable ones. A bench on a hard day, a slow stretch with a companion, the first light after a bad night. The peace is there with the sore feet. It does not wait for them to be cured.
Later in the same chapter Thomas has a phrase for the reader:
a wayfaring man

. It is an old word for someone on the road. Such a person, he says, may have abundance of peace, as much as is possible for someone who is only a wayfarer. That is both realistic and gentle. It does not promise the peace of the destination. It promises the peace of the road, which is real, and partial, and enough to go on with.

Where is it hard? The passage pairs peace with humility, and that pairing can sound like a test you might fail. If you are anxious, are you proud? Plainly not. Anxiety and pride are different things, and many humble people lie awake. The sentence is better read as a description than as a verdict: it tells you where peace tends to be found, and it does not tell you that you have been refused. Nor does it mean that you should stop caring about justice or change. It says only that peace and perfect conditions are two separate things.

Another hard place is the idea that perfect peace is not available here at all. Some readers will find that sobering and some, a relief. If the state of complete rest belongs to another life, what is the point of looking for any now? The answer in the passage is that partial peace is real, and the road is where it lives.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? That you look, once, in the middle of something imperfect, for the small peace that is already there. The sock with the hole. The bed that is a little too hard. A friend who is difficult. Under the minor trouble is often a stillness that was waiting for you to stop waiting for conditions.
For the walk

items.t: Where, today, is there some peace in the middle of something imperfect? It may be very small.

At the next moment of mild discomfort, tired legs, a slight chill, a delay, pause and look for the small peace that is present alongside it. You do not have to make it larger. Say, quietly, "This too," and stay with it for three breaths before you walk on.

spans.t: At the end of the day
The room is quiet, or quiet enough. Another day has gone, and this one was not perfect, and you are somehow at the start of the third week. Sit for a minute, and do nothing about it.

Look back over the day for its moments of peace, and be careful how you look. The easy ones are obvious: the view, the shower, the meal. Those are real, and worth naming. But look for the harder kind too: a moment of quiet that came in the middle of something uncomfortable. A calm that arrived while your feet hurt. A moment of ease in a crowded room. A conversation in which you were tired and, to your own surprise, did not mind. Those are the ones the passage is talking about, and they are often easier to miss.

Now ask what you were waiting for. Many of us hold a private list of conditions for peace: when the feet stop hurting, when the next stage is booked, when the weather turns, when that conversation is behind me. It is worth looking at the list. Some of the items may not be needed. Some may be keeping you from a peace that was on offer an hour ago.
And what disquiet did the day hold? Say it plainly. It need not be solved. It is enough to see that it can sit in the same room as a small peace without either of them having to leave.

If you have begun to count down to the end of your walk, notice that the countdown is also a condition: I will rest when I arrive. It is a very natural one, and a very common one, and it can make the last days a long wait. The passage suggests that the peace on offer is not at the end of the road. It is on it.

A small practice for the night: put a hand on your chest or your stomach, feel the breath going in and out, and say to yourself, "This is enough for tonight." If that feels silly, try it anyway. Silly is allowed.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: Where did I wait for conditions to be perfect before allowing myself to rest?
What small peace was present today alongside something uncomfortable?
What am I trying to get away from tonight, and could it simply be allowed to be here?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. The end of a day is not a test of how peaceful you are. If you are tired and irritable, you are tired and irritable, and that has little to do with the state of your soul. Peace that is real can look quite ordinary in the evening: a lowered shoulder, a long breath, the plain fact of being horizontal. Do not ask for more tonight than that.
A short prayer

Let there be peace tonight, even if it is only a small one. Not because everything is right, but because I am here, and the day is over, and the bed is soft enough. Let the trouble sit quietly beside me, and not climb in. Let me be a wayfarer, and not ask the road to be a home.

chapters.title: Day 16. My planning can profit but little

spans.t: What would it be like to plan a little less and trust a little more?
The passage

paras.t: “My Son, always commit thy cause to Me; I will dispose it aright in due time. Wait for My arrangement of it, and then thou shalt find it for thy profit.” … O Lord, right freely I commit all things to Thee; for my planning can profit but little. Oh that I did not dwell so much on future events, but could offer myself altogether to Thy pleasures without delay. … My Son, a man often striveth vehemently after somewhat which he desireth; but when he hath obtained it he beginneth to be of another mind, because his affections towards it are not lasting, but rather rush on from one thing to another.

spans.t: Reflection

Every pilgrim has a plan, and every plan has a short life. It begins at home, with a spreadsheet or a pencilled table of stages, distances, beds and cafés. It survives the first few days. Then comes a storm, or a blister, or a friend who wants to go on, or a bed that turns out to be full, and the plan is revised. After the third revision it is hardly a plan any more, just a direction. Walkers have a saying for the process, that the Way provides. It is half a joke and half a confession: we learned that our arrangements were not the only ones being made.
Thomas à Kempis has a short passage on this, and it has two voices in it. The first is the voice that speaks to the disciple in his third book:
always commit thy cause to Me; I will dispose it aright in due time. Wait for My arrangement of it.
The second is the disciple's reply, which is honest and a little rueful. He agrees freely. His planning, he admits, can profit but little. If only he did not dwell so much on future events.

It is an easy thing to misread. Thomas is not saying that you should stop thinking ahead. A person who walks into August without a bed is not being trusting, only hopeful. His point is about what planning can do. Planning prepares. It does not control. It can get you to the starting line, but it cannot arrange the weather, or the knee, or the person you will meet. The mistake is to put all your weight on it, and then be shaken when it gives way.

The wise path, in practice, is to plan and then loosen your grip. Make the arrangements you can. Look at tomorrow's stage, see where the water is, know the next town. Then let the day have its say. That small letting-go is nearly all of what Thomas means by waiting. It is the half-second at the fork in the path when you allow that the road may know something you do not.

The third part of the passage turns, quite unexpectedly, to desire. A person often strives hard for something, he says, and when he has it, he begins to be of another mind. His affection for the thing is not lasting. It runs on, from one object to the next. Anyone who has wanted a shower for six hours and then barely noticed it knows this. And anyone who has been dreaming of the end of the walk, the cathedral, the certificate, the long sleep, may be quietly preparing for a surprise. The thing we strive for does not always turn out to be what we wanted. The passage does not say this to spoil it. It says it so you will not be caught unawares.

Where is it hard? The word "wait" is a difficult one for people with practical problems. Someone with a sick parent, a bill, a legal matter, a decision with a deadline, cannot simply wait for it to be arranged. Nor should they. Thomas's advice is not an excuse for neglecting what is in your own hands. It is better read as a counsel for the part that is not: do everything within reach, and then do not carry the remainder as if it were all on your own back.

There is also a doubt that deserves to be said out loud. "I will dispose it aright" is a promise, and not every reader will feel that it is kept. People commit their cause and it goes badly. Thomas knows this as well as anyone. The passage does not say that all will be well. It says that the burden of arranging the world is not yours alone, and that is a modest claim, and a lighter one than it sounds.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Plan once, in the morning, and then stop. Allow the day one change. At the first fork, wait a few seconds before choosing. Leave the stage app in your pocket for an hour. See what the road suggests when you are not busy telling it what to do.
For the walk

items.t: What am I trying to control today that I could only prepare for? Name it, and then name the one thing about it that is actually yours to do.

Make the day's plan once, this morning, and then put it away. Allow the day one change, and when you come to the next fork or the next decision, wait three breaths before you choose. Notice what the day offers that was not on the plan.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Tonight's bed may be the one you planned, or one you arrived at by an accident, or one you were very glad of at the end of a day that did not follow the schedule. Whichever it is, you are in it, and that is a small proof of what the passage says: it was arranged somehow.

Look back at the day and set your plan beside what happened. The two are rarely the same. Where did they part? Perhaps the morning stage was longer than expected, or shorter. Perhaps a person turned up that you had not meant to meet, or a place you meant to see was closed. Perhaps you changed your mind at a crossing and went another way. Some of those changes will have been annoying. Some, when you look at them now, may have been gifts. It is worth noticing, without insisting on a tidy moral, which was which.

Notice, too, how your body felt about the changes. Some people find a change of plan a relief, and some find it a small crisis. Neither is wrong, and knowing which you are is useful for the days ahead. A plan held loosely has one pleasant side effect: when it works, it feels like a gift, and when it fails, it feels like weather.

Now think about tomorrow, and be careful. The mind loves to begin planning at exactly the hour when it is least able to plan well. It will draw up a perfect itinerary at ten at night, and shred it at seven the next morning. Try giving tomorrow a single line: where you hope to be, roughly, by evening. That is plenty. The rest can be arranged by the day.

And the third part of the passage: is there something you wanted a great deal that you now have, and find strangely ordinary? Perhaps it was a bed, a meal, a rest, a view. Perhaps it was something larger. Hold it up for a moment and notice what happened to the wanting.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I plan today that did not happen, and what happened instead?
What am I planning tonight that I could leave until morning?
What did I want so much that, once I had it, I began wanting something else?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. A tired mind plans badly and worries well. If you find yourself running through tomorrow's difficulties in detail, you are probably not solving anything. You are only rehearsing. Put the plan down. It will be exactly as useful in the morning, and you will be better equipped to make it.
A short prayer

Let me do what is mine to do, and put down the rest. Teach me to plan lightly and to wait without fretting. Let tomorrow be arranged by hands wiser than mine, and let me be glad of the surprise. Let me not want so hard that I cannot enjoy what I have. Tonight, let me simply lie down in the arrangement of the day.
What could you give away today, and what would giving free?
The passage

paras.t: “Strive, My Son, to do another’s will rather than thine own. Choose always to have less rather than more. Seek always after the lowest place, and to be subject to all. Wish always and pray that the will of God be fulfilled in thee. Behold, such a man as this entereth into the inheritance of peace and quietness.” … O my Lord, this Thy short discourse hath in itself much of perfectness. It is short in words but full of meaning, and abundant in fruit.

spans.t: Reflection

Many hostels have a shelf by the door, or a box in a corner, where walkers leave what they no longer want to carry. It is a small museum of changed minds. A second pair of trousers. A paperback with a bookmark halfway through. A bottle of sun cream, a jar of olives, a pair of poles with the rubber worn smooth. Each item on it was once thought essential, and each was set down somewhere between the first week and the third. Someone else will pick it up. Nobody arranged it. It simply happens, in many hostels, most days.

That shelf is a very good commentary on the passage. The voice in this chapter, which is the one Thomas à Kempis gives to God in his third book, promises to teach the way of peace and of true liberty, and it does so in four short sentences. Do another's will rather than your own. Choose to have less rather than more. Seek the lowest place and be subject to all. Wish and pray that the will of God be done in you. The man who does this, it says, enters into an inheritance of peace and quietness.

Then the disciple replies, and his reply is lovely. It is a short discourse, he says, much in few words, and abundant in fruit. If he could keep it fully, he adds in the next line, disturbance would not arise within him so easily. It is the plain testimony of someone who has tried it and knows how far he falls short.

Lay the four sentences against a long walk. The first is about yielding: letting someone go first through the door, give the better seat, choose the other's restaurant. The second is the pack, which every walker eventually learns: you can get along on less than you set out with, and you feel lighter for it. The third is the oddest, to take the lowest place. It means, perhaps, to be at the end of the queue, to take the top bunk, to be last to be served. And the fourth is the largest: to hold your own plan loosely under something bigger.

The thread through all four is offering. You give something up, a preference, a thing, a place, and in the giving something unexpectedly lightens. A person who offers the lower bunk to someone with bad knees often sleeps well in the upper. A person who gives away half a loaf rarely goes hungry. It is one of the paradoxes of the road that the hands which open are the ones that are filled.
Where is it hard? Seriously hard, and it needs honesty. "Do another's will rather than thine own",
always

, is a dangerous sentence in some hands. There are people who give way all the time, who have never had the luxury of wanting anything for themselves, and to whom this advice would be one more weight. If you are someone who is already the first to yield, this passage is not aimed at you. For you the beginning of the lesson may be to ask what you want, and to say so. Thomas is writing to people who grasp, and a cloister full of the grasping is a very different place from a kitchen full of the over-giving.

In the same way, "the lowest place" is a hard phrase for anyone who has never been offered a high one. It is not an instruction to be walked over, and it does not ask you to put up with harm. It is a way of saying that you do not need to win the seat to be at peace.

There is a plain doubt, too. Is "less rather than more" always wise? A tired person who gives up the last of the water is not being holy. The passage asks for a certain freedom from grasping, not for foolishness. Giving that is real begins with enough to give.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? One small yielding. One small lightening. Let somebody go first. Offer the better seat. Look in your pack for a single thing you could do without, and put it on the shelf for the next person.
For the walk

items.t: What could I give away today, and what would I be freed by giving? The answer may be quite a small thing.

Make one small yielding before the next stop: let someone go first, offer a seat, take the less comfortable place. And look in your pack, or in your head, for one thing you do not need, and decide to leave it behind. If it is a thing, put it where someone else can find it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Look at the little pile of the day's possessions: boots by the bed, pack at the foot, a few things on a hook. It is not very much. Many walkers say, after a few weeks, that it is more than enough, and that they had never guessed how little a body needs to be warm, dry and fed.

Think back through the day for the moments of giving and taking. Where did you give way? Perhaps over a small thing: a place in a line, a seat at the table, the choice of where to eat, the decision about the next day's start. Was it freely given, or did it come out sideways, as resentment? Giving that is done with a sour face is not what the passage means. If it was freely done, let yourself enjoy it for a moment. It is a quiet pleasure, and it is allowed.

And where did you hold on? There is usually something. A view you insisted on, a bed you would not swap, a plan you kept to against the evidence. Ask what you were protecting. Often it is something small and tired, a fear of being overlooked, or of not having enough. It can be looked at kindly.

If there was a moment today when you found yourself giving too much, doing the whole of the kitchen, making all the choices, saying yes when you meant no, notice that too. The passage is not asking for that, and you are allowed to rest.

The pack is a good mirror. Which things did you reach for today, and which sat untouched at the bottom? You do not have to decide anything tonight, but it is worth noticing. And there is a heavier pack that you carry in your head: a grievance, a rehearsed argument, a comparison. These weigh nothing on a scale and a great deal on a hill. Naming one you could leave behind tomorrow is enough.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: Where did I give way today, and was it freely given?
Where did I hold on to my own will, and what was I protecting?
What could I leave behind tomorrow, in my pack or in my head?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. Giving takes energy, and tonight you may have very little. You are not obliged to be generous at ten o'clock. A tired person's first and best gift is to be good company in the most ordinary way: a courteous word, a quiet room. Tomorrow will bring other chances. Tonight, it is enough not to take what is not yours.
A short prayer

Teach me to hold things lightly: the seat, the plan, the pack, the point I wanted to win. Where I gave today, let it have been gladly. Where I grasped, forgive me. Let me not give so much that I vanish, nor keep so much that I cannot move. Let there be room in my hands for what comes tomorrow.
What will you carry home from the place you walked to?
The passage

paras.t: Many run to diverse places to visit the memorials of departed Saints, and rejoice to hear of their deeds and to look upon the beautiful buildings of their shrines. … Often in looking at those memorials men are moved by curiosity and novelty, and very little fruit of amendment is borne away, especially when there is so much careless trifling and so little true contrition.

spans.t: Reflection

The end of a pilgrimage has a particular noise. There is the square, wide and stone and full of people, and a great many of them are photographing each other. Some have walked for weeks, with the sunburn and the lean look to show for it, and some stepped off a coach twenty minutes ago. There are rucksacks stacked against the walls, and hugging, and the odd person lying flat on their back with their arms spread. It is joyful and tiring and slightly bewildering. Somebody is playing music. Everybody has, at once, arrived.

Whichever day you reach your own end, a cathedral square or a kitchen door, you will probably meet a version of it, and Thomas à Kempis has a sharp word for the moment. Many people run to various places, he says, to visit the memorials of departed saints, to hear of their deeds and look at the handsome buildings of their shrines. And then, in a second sentence: often, looking at those memorials, people are moved by curiosity and novelty, and very little fruit of amendment is borne away.
Amendment is the old word for change, for a life a little better afterwards. Thomas is asking a plain question. What goes home with you? Not what you saw. What you carry.

Note first where this sentence sits. It comes from the fourth book, in the chapter on receiving communion. In the sentence that we have left out, Thomas turns from shrines to the Sacrament, which is the subject of the fourth book, and sets it above any shrine. That sentence belongs to readers who share his faith, and this reading will not try to explain it or argue with it. What remains is the question about fruit, and that stands on its own.

It is a hard thing to be asked at the end of a long walk. You are tired, and perhaps moved, and a little giddy, and here is a man from the fifteenth century wondering whether any of this will make a difference. It sounds almost rude. But it is a good question, and it does not accuse you of anything. Pilgrimage has long had its sightseers and its seekers, and they are often the same people, on different days of the same road. Curiosity is human. Nobody is wrong to admire an old building, or to be curious about the person it remembers. The question is only what, in the end, you take away.

The hard word in the passage is "careless trifling". It would be easy to use it as a stick against the crowd in the square, and to feel a quiet superiority over the people who arrived by coach. That would be a mistake of the kind Thomas is always warning about. We are all a mixture of trifling and seeking, in the same hour, in the same body. A person with a camera may be quietly overwhelmed. A person with a rucksack may be thinking about lunch.

The passage also talks of "true contrition", of real sorrow for what has been wrong. That is a heavy phrase for a first-time reader, and not everyone will recognise it as their own. Take it more simply, if you like. A walk of this length tends to show a person things about themselves. The question is what you do with what you saw.

Fruit, in this sense, is quite small. It is not a transformation. It is something like: I will walk more slowly. I will ring my sister. I will stop saying yes to everything. I will not carry that grudge into the new year. A small, definite thing, chosen before you leave, and taken home like a stone in a pocket.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Whichever day you reach the place you were walking to, do not let the noise decide for you. Before you leave, find a quiet corner, a pew, a step, a wall, and sit for a few minutes. Ask what you would like to carry home, and let it be one thing.
For the walk

items.t: If I could take one small change home from this walk, what would it be?

Before you leave the place you were walking to, find a quiet corner and sit for five minutes. Do not decide yet what the change is. Only ask the question, and see what rises. If you like, write one line on a scrap of paper and put it in your pocket.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The evening after an arrival has its own odd flavour. You are probably tired in a way that is hard to describe: not the tiredness of the legs, which are full of pleasant complaint, but a more general exhaustion, as if you had been feeling things for several days without a break. You may also feel a little flat. People do. The great thing has happened, and the world has gone on, and there is a plate of ordinary food in front of you.

Look back over the day for what was actually there, and not for what was supposed to be. There may have been a moment of real feeling, in the square, in the church, in the face of someone you walked with. There may have been a stretch of noise and photographs and a sense of unreality. There may have been nothing special at all, and then, an hour later, in the middle of something quite ordinary, a lump in the throat. All of that is the day. None of it is wrong.

Think about what you came for. It may be that you set out for one reason and found another. It may be that you cannot say, even now. Ask whether it is still the same. There is no correct answer. The passage only wants you to ask, and to take the answer seriously.

And think of who is at home, and what you would like them to know. Not the facts of the trip, which can be told in an hour, but the thing you would like them to see in you. It may be easier to tell a friend than to tell yourself.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I come for, and is it the same as what I found?
What one small change do I want to carry home?
Who do I want to tell about this walk, and what do I want to say?

spans.t: An honest word about tiredness. After an arrival there is a very large tiredness, and a very large amount of feeling. Do not try to settle the meaning of the walk tonight. It will take weeks, perhaps years, to see what it was. For now it is enough to eat, to sleep, and to know that you got here. The fruit, as the passage says, is borne away. It does not have to be picked tonight.
A short prayer

Thank you for the road and for the place it led to. Let me not mistake the noise for the fruit. Show me, when I am rested, one small thing to carry home, and give me the courage to keep it. Let those who arrived with me, and those who did not, be held in the same gentle light. Let me sleep, and let the walk sink in.
